modules.title: The Monaco Qiskit editor overview

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

modules.title: The Bloch Sphere view overview

content.text: The Bloch sphere is a picture that turns any single-qubit state into a point on a sphere, making superposition and gates visually intuitive.

Every pure single-qubit state maps to a point on the surface of a unit sphere. The north pole is |0>, the south pole is |1>, and points on the equator are equal superpositions such as |+>, |->, |+i> and |-i>.

A state is fixed by two angles: theta, the polar angle from the north pole, and phi, the azimuthal angle around the equator. The state is cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi) sin(theta/2)|1>. The angle phi is the relative phase.

Single-qubit gates are rotations of this sphere. X, Y and Z are 180-degree rotations about their axes; the rotation gates rx, ry, rz turn by any angle. This is why visualising gates as rotations is so powerful.

items: North pole = |0>, south pole = |1>
Equator = equal superpositions
Angles theta (polar) and phi (phase) fix the state
Gates are rotations of the sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is like a globe where your qubit is a pin; gates spin the globe to move the pin to a new latitude and longitude.
The state |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 sits on the equator at phi = 0 (theta = 90 degrees). Applying Z moves it to |-> on the opposite side of the equator (phi = 180 degrees).

items: Forgetting the half-angle (theta/2) in the amplitudes.
Trying to draw two entangled qubits on one Bloch sphere -- it only works for a single, unentangled qubit.

modules.title: Reading a measurement histogram

content.text: Measurement is how a quantum state becomes a classical result. It is probabilistic, irreversible, and the only non-unitary step in a quantum circuit.

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, you get 0 or 1 with probabilities given by the Born rule (|amplitude|^2). The act of measuring collapses the state onto the outcome you saw: after measuring 1, the qubit is now exactly |1>.

Collapse is irreversible and destroys the superposition, so you cannot read the amplitudes directly. To learn the distribution you prepare and measure the same circuit many times (shots) and build a histogram of outcomes.
You can measure in other bases too. Measuring in the X basis is done by applying a Hadamard first and then measuring in the Z basis, which is how you probe phase information that the Z basis hides.

items: Outcome probability = |amplitude|^2
Measurement collapses the state onto the result
It is irreversible and destroys superposition
Repeat many shots to see the distribution
Change basis by rotating before measuring

content.text: Measurement is like opening a wrapped gift: before opening, several possibilities exist; opening fixes one and you cannot un-open it.

(|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 --[measure]--> 0  (state now |0>)
                           or  1  (state now |1>)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)
result = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())   # about {'0': 500, '1': 500}
Measuring |+> once might give 0; the qubit then collapses to |0>, and measuring again immediately gives 0 with certainty. The randomness was in the first measurement only.

items: Expecting a single measurement to reveal the amplitudes -- it only gives one random outcome.

modules.title: Introduction to imaginary numbers

content.text: Complex numbers are the native language of quantum mechanics. Every amplitude that describes a quantum state is a complex number, so this topic is a true prerequisite for everything that follows.

A complex number has the form z = a + b*i, where a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, and i is the imaginary unit defined by i*i = -1. You can picture z as a point (a, b) in a two-dimensional plane called the complex plane, with the real axis horizontal and the imaginary axis vertical.

Two descriptions of the same number are equally useful. The rectangular form a + b*i is best for adding and subtracting. The polar form r*(cos(theta) + i*sin(theta)) is best for multiplying, because multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their magnitudes r and adds their angles theta.

The magnitude (or modulus) is |z| = sqrt(a*a + b*b), the distance from the origin. The angle theta is called the phase. In quantum computing the magnitude squared gives a probability, while the phase, though invisible to a single measurement, drives interference between paths.

The complex conjugate of z = a + b*i is z* = a - b*i (flip the sign of the imaginary part). A key identity is z * z* = |z|^2, a non-negative real number -- this is exactly how amplitudes turn into probabilities.

items: z = a + b*i with i*i = -1
|z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) is the magnitude
Phase theta is the angle in the complex plane
z * z* = |z|^2 gives a real probability
Multiply: magnitudes multiply, phases add

content.text: Think of a complex number as an arrow on a clock face: its length is the magnitude and the direction it points is the phase. Multiplying by another number stretches the arrow and spins it.
Take z = 3 + 4i. Magnitude = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Conjugate z* = 3 - 4i. Then z * z* = 9 + 16 = 25 = |z|^2, a real number, exactly as expected.

Euler's formula e^(i*theta) = cos(theta) + i*sin(theta) packs the polar form into a single exponential and is the reason phases and rotations are so clean in quantum mechanics -- you will meet it again in rotation gates.

items: Writing i*i = +1 instead of -1.
Forgetting that the probability uses the magnitude SQUARED, not the magnitude.

modules.title: Modulus of a complex number

content.text: Complex numbers are the native language of quantum mechanics. Every amplitude that describes a quantum state is a complex number, so this topic is a true prerequisite for everything that follows.

The complex conjugate of z = a + b*i is z* = a - b*i (flip the sign of the imaginary part). A key identity is z * z* = |z|^2, a non-negative real number -- this is exactly how amplitudes turn into probabilities.

modules.title: Euler formula e^(i-theta)

content.text: Euler's formula links exponentials, trigonometry and complex numbers in one elegant equation, and it is the cleanest way to write quantum phases and rotations.
Euler's formula states e^(i*theta) = cos(theta) + i*sin(theta). It says that raising e to an imaginary power traces out the unit circle in the complex plane as theta increases.

This means any complex number of magnitude r and phase theta can be written as r*e^(i*theta). Multiplication becomes trivial: r1*e^(i*a) times r2*e^(i*b) = r1*r2*e^(i*(a+b)), so magnitudes multiply and phases add.

In quantum computing a phase factor e^(i*theta) multiplies an amplitude without changing its magnitude, so it leaves single-shot probabilities unchanged but controls interference. Every rotation and phase gate is built from such exponentials.

items: e^(i*theta) = cos(theta) + i*sin(theta)
Polar form r*e^(i*theta)
Phases add under multiplication
A pure phase does not change probabilities but drives interference

content.text: e^(i*theta) is a point walking around a unit circle; theta is how far around it has walked.

e^(i*theta) walks around the unit circle:

        e^(i*pi/2) = i
              |
 e^(i*pi)=-1 -+- e^(i*0)=1
              |
        e^(i*3pi/2) = -i
At theta = pi, e^(i*pi) = cos(pi) + i*sin(pi) = -1 + 0i = -1. This is the famous identity e^(i*pi) + 1 = 0.

modules.title: Why complex numbers matter in quantum computing

content.text: Complex numbers are the native language of quantum mechanics. Every amplitude that describes a quantum state is a complex number, so this topic is a true prerequisite for everything that follows.

A complex number has the form z = a + b*i, where a is the real part, b is the imaginary part, and i is the imaginary unit defined by i*i = -1. You can picture z as a point (a, b) in a two-dimensional plane called the complex plane, with the real axis horizontal and the imaginary axis vertical.

Two descriptions of the same number are equally useful. The rectangular form a + b*i is best for adding and subtracting. The polar form r*(cos(theta) + i*sin(theta)) is best for multiplying, because multiplying two complex numbers multiplies their magnitudes r and adds their angles theta.

The magnitude (or modulus) is |z| = sqrt(a*a + b*b), the distance from the origin. The angle theta is called the phase. In quantum computing the magnitude squared gives a probability, while the phase, though invisible to a single measurement, drives interference between paths.

The complex conjugate of z = a + b*i is z* = a - b*i (flip the sign of the imaginary part). A key identity is z * z* = |z|^2, a non-negative real number -- this is exactly how amplitudes turn into probabilities.

items: z = a + b*i with i*i = -1
|z| = sqrt(a^2 + b^2) is the magnitude
Phase theta is the angle in the complex plane
z * z* = |z|^2 gives a real probability
Multiply: magnitudes multiply, phases add

content.text: Think of a complex number as an arrow on a clock face: its length is the magnitude and the direction it points is the phase. Multiplying by another number stretches the arrow and spins it.
Take z = 3 + 4i. Magnitude = sqrt(9 + 16) = sqrt(25) = 5. Conjugate z* = 3 - 4i. Then z * z* = 9 + 16 = 25 = |z|^2, a real number, exactly as expected.

Euler's formula e^(i*theta) = cos(theta) + i*sin(theta) packs the polar form into a single exponential and is the reason phases and rotations are so clean in quantum mechanics -- you will meet it again in rotation gates.

modules.title: Angles, radians and degrees

content.text: Angles are measured in radians throughout quantum computing because rotation gates take their angles in radians. Getting comfortable with radians now prevents a lot of later confusion.
A radian is the angle you get when the arc length equals the radius. A full circle is 2*pi radians, which equals 360 degrees, so 180 degrees = pi radians and 90 degrees = pi/2 radians.
To convert, multiply degrees by pi/180 to get radians, or multiply radians by 180/pi to get degrees. Qiskit rotation gates (rx, ry, rz) always expect radians.
Because the Bloch sphere is a sphere, qubit positions and gate rotations are naturally described by angles, so radians appear constantly.

modules.title: Sine, cosine and tangent refresher

content.text: Sine and cosine describe how a qubit's amplitudes split between |0> and |1>, and how rotation gates move a state. They are the trigonometry backbone of single-qubit behaviour.
For a right triangle, sine of an angle is opposite over hypotenuse and cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse. On the unit circle, a point at angle theta has coordinates (cos(theta), sin(theta)).

A general single-qubit state can be written as cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi)*sin(theta/2)|1>. The cosine controls how much |0> is present and the sine controls how much |1> is present, with theta the polar angle on the Bloch sphere.
Because cos^2 + sin^2 = 1, the probabilities of measuring 0 and 1 automatically add to 1 -- the trigonometric identity guarantees normalisation.

items: cos^2(x) + sin^2(x) = 1
State: cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi) sin(theta/2)|1>
cos controls the |0> weight, sin controls the |1> weight
Unit circle point: (cos theta, sin theta)

content.text: Sine and cosine are the shadows of a spinning point -- as the point goes around the circle, its horizontal shadow is cosine and its vertical shadow is sine.
At theta = 90 degrees (pi/2 radians) on the Bloch sphere, the state is cos(45deg)|0> + sin(45deg)|1> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2, the equal superposition |+>.

modules.title: What is a vector

content.text: A quantum state is a vector. Learning to read, add and normalise vectors lets you treat any qubit state as a concrete list of numbers you can compute with.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, often written as a column. A single qubit lives in a two-dimensional complex vector space, so its state is a column of two complex numbers [alpha, beta], meaning alpha|0> + beta|1>.
You add vectors component by component and scale them by multiplying every entry by a number. Superposition is literally vector addition: |+> = (1/sqrt2)([1,0] + [0,1]) = [1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2].
The length (norm) of a state vector must be 1. For [alpha, beta] this means |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1, which is the normalisation condition guaranteeing the probabilities add to one.

items: A qubit state is a 2-entry complex vector [alpha, beta]
Add vectors entrywise; scale by a scalar
Norm must equal 1: |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1

content.text: A state vector is like a recipe: each entry is how much of each basis ingredient (|0> and |1>) to mix in.
The state 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> is the vector [0.6, 0.8]. Check the norm: 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, so it is a valid state. Measuring gives 0 with probability 0.36 and 1 with probability 0.64.

modules.title: The dot / inner product

content.text: The inner product measures overlap between two states and is written cleanly in Dirac (bra-ket) notation. It tells you how similar two states are and underpins measurement probabilities.

In Dirac notation a state (a column vector) is a ket |psi>, and its conjugate-transpose (a row vector) is a bra <psi|. The inner product of |phi> and |psi> is written <phi|psi> and is a single complex number.
To compute <phi|psi> you take the conjugate of each entry of |phi>, line them up with the entries of |psi>, multiply pairwise and sum. The result measures how much the two states overlap.

Two states are orthogonal when their inner product is 0, meaning they are perfectly distinguishable. The basis states satisfy <0|0> = 1, <1|1> = 1 and <0|1> = 0. The probability of measuring state |phi> given state |psi> is |<phi|psi>|^2.

<phi|psi> is a single complex number (overlap)
Orthogonal means <phi|psi> = 0
Probability = |<phi|psi>|^2

content.text: The inner product is like asking 'how much do these two arrows point the same way?' -- 1 means identical, 0 means at right angles (completely different).

<phi|  =  [ a*  b* ]   (row, conjugated)

|psi> =  [ c ]
         [ d ]

<phi|psi> = a*c + b*d
Overlap of |0> and |+>: <0|+> = <0| (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 = (1 + 0)/sqrt2 = 1/sqrt2. So the probability of measuring 0 in state |+> is |1/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5.

modules.title: Matrix-vector multiplication

content.text: A quantum state is a vector. Learning to read, add and normalise vectors lets you treat any qubit state as a concrete list of numbers you can compute with.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, often written as a column. A single qubit lives in a two-dimensional complex vector space, so its state is a column of two complex numbers [alpha, beta], meaning alpha|0> + beta|1>.
You add vectors component by component and scale them by multiplying every entry by a number. Superposition is literally vector addition: |+> = (1/sqrt2)([1,0] + [0,1]) = [1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2].
The length (norm) of a state vector must be 1. For [alpha, beta] this means |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1, which is the normalisation condition guaranteeing the probabilities add to one.

items: A qubit state is a 2-entry complex vector [alpha, beta]
Add vectors entrywise; scale by a scalar
Norm must equal 1: |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1

content.text: A state vector is like a recipe: each entry is how much of each basis ingredient (|0> and |1>) to mix in.
The state 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> is the vector [0.6, 0.8]. Check the norm: 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, so it is a valid state. Measuring gives 0 with probability 0.36 and 1 with probability 0.64.

items: Using an un-normalised vector -- always check the entries squared add to 1.

modules.title: Matrix-matrix multiplication

content.text: Matrices are how quantum gates are written, and matrix multiplication is how a gate acts on a state. Master this and every gate becomes a concrete calculation.

A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers. A single-qubit gate is a 2x2 complex matrix; an n-qubit gate is a 2^n by 2^n matrix. Applying a gate to a state means multiplying the gate matrix by the state vector.

To multiply a 2x2 matrix by a 2-entry vector, each output entry is the dot product of a matrix row with the vector. Order matters: gates applied later sit to the left in the product, so the circuit G2 then G1 is written G1*G2 as matrices.
Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative: A*B is usually different from B*A. This non-commuting behaviour is why the order of quantum gates changes the result.

content.text: Eigenvectors are the special states a gate leaves pointing in the same direction, and eigenvalues say by how much they are scaled. They explain gate behaviour and are central to phase estimation.
For a matrix A, an eigenvector v satisfies A*v = lambda*v, where the number lambda is the eigenvalue. The gate does not rotate v into a new direction, it only scales it by lambda.
For a unitary gate every eigenvalue has magnitude 1, so it can be written as e^(i*theta). The phase theta is exactly what the phase-estimation algorithm is designed to read out.

Eigen-decomposition lets you understand a gate by its action on its eigenvectors. For example, Z has eigenvector |0> with eigenvalue +1 and eigenvector |1> with eigenvalue -1, which is just a restatement of Z|0>=|0> and Z|1>=-|1>.

items: A*v = lambda*v: v is the eigenvector, lambda the eigenvalue
Unitary eigenvalues have magnitude 1 (e^(i*theta))
Eigenvectors are directions the gate only scales
Phase estimation reads the eigenvalue phase

content.text: Eigenvectors are the axes a spinning object can rotate around without wobbling -- the object just turns along them cleanly.
For Z, |1> is an eigenvector: Z|1> = -|1>, so the eigenvalue is -1 = e^(i*pi). Its phase pi is what phase estimation would return.

items: Expecting a gate to rotate its own eigenvectors -- it only scales them.

modules.title: The tensor (Kronecker) product

content.text: The tensor product is how the states of separate qubits combine into one joint state. It is the reason quantum computers scale exponentially.

To describe two qubits together you take the tensor (Kronecker) product of their individual state vectors. Two 2-entry vectors combine into a single 4-entry vector whose basis states are |00>, |01>, |10>, |11>.

Each added qubit doubles the dimension: 1 qubit is 2 numbers, 2 qubits are 4, 3 qubits are 8, and n qubits need 2^n complex numbers. This exponential growth is the source of quantum computing's potential power and of the difficulty of simulating it classically.
Gates on separate qubits also combine by tensor product. If you apply H to qubit 0 and nothing (I) to qubit 1, the joint gate is H tensor I, a 4x4 matrix.

items: Combine qubit states with the tensor product
n qubits need 2^n amplitudes
Separate gates combine as A tensor B
Exponential growth = quantum scaling

content.text: The tensor product is like listing every combination on a menu: 2 starters and 2 mains give 4 full meals, 3 and 3 give 9, and so on.
|0> tensor |1> = [1,0] tensor [0,1] = [0,1,0,0] = |01>. The single 1 sits in the position labelled 01, confirming the combined state is |01>.

items: Adding the dimensions (2+2) instead of multiplying them (2*2=4).

modules.title: Probability basics and sample spaces

content.text: Measurement outcomes are random, and the Born rule tells you their probabilities. This is the bridge from a quantum state to the histogram the simulator shows you.

The Born rule states that the probability of measuring a particular basis outcome equals the squared magnitude of that outcome's amplitude. For alpha|0> + beta|1>, you get 0 with probability |alpha|^2 and 1 with probability |beta|^2.

Because the state is normalised, these probabilities add to 1. A single measurement gives one random outcome and collapses the state; to see the full distribution you run many shots and build a histogram.
The expectation value is the average outcome weighted by probability. For an observable it is computed as <psi|A|psi> and is what many algorithms, such as VQE, actually try to minimise.

items: Probability = |amplitude|^2 (Born rule)
Probabilities add to 1
One shot gives one random outcome and collapses the state
Many shots build a histogram
Expectation value = <psi|A|psi>

content.text: A quantum state is like a weighted dice: the amplitudes squared are the chances of each face, and each roll (shot) gives just one face.

state: alpha|0> + beta|1>

P(0) = |alpha|^2
P(1) = |beta|^2
P(0) + P(1) = 1
For (|0> + i|1>)/sqrt2, alpha = 1/sqrt2 and beta = i/sqrt2. P(0) = |1/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5 and P(1) = |i/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5, so the histogram over many shots is about half 0 and half 1.

items: Using the amplitude itself instead of its squared magnitude for the probability.
Forgetting that a phase like i does not change a single-measurement probability.

modules.title: NumPy dot product and matmul

content.text: The inner product measures overlap between two states and is written cleanly in Dirac (bra-ket) notation. It tells you how similar two states are and underpins measurement probabilities.

In Dirac notation a state (a column vector) is a ket |psi>, and its conjugate-transpose (a row vector) is a bra <psi|. The inner product of |phi> and |psi> is written <phi|psi> and is a single complex number.
To compute <phi|psi> you take the conjugate of each entry of |phi>, line them up with the entries of |psi>, multiply pairwise and sum. The result measures how much the two states overlap.

Two states are orthogonal when their inner product is 0, meaning they are perfectly distinguishable. The basis states satisfy <0|0> = 1, <1|1> = 1 and <0|1> = 0. The probability of measuring state |phi> given state |psi> is |<phi|psi>|^2.

items: Ket |psi> is a column, bra <psi| is its conjugate-transpose row
<phi|psi> is a single complex number (overlap)
Orthogonal means <phi|psi> = 0
Probability = |<phi|psi>|^2

content.text: The inner product is like asking 'how much do these two arrows point the same way?' -- 1 means identical, 0 means at right angles (completely different).

<phi|  =  [ a*  b* ]   (row, conjugated)

|psi> =  [ c ]
         [ d ]

<phi|psi> = a*c + b*d
Overlap of |0> and |+>: <0|+> = <0| (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 = (1 + 0)/sqrt2 = 1/sqrt2. So the probability of measuring 0 in state |+> is |1/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5.

items: Forgetting to conjugate the bra entries.
Confusing the inner product <phi|psi> (a number) with the outer product |psi><phi| (a matrix).

modules.title: NumPy kron for tensor products

content.text: The tensor product is how the states of separate qubits combine into one joint state. It is the reason quantum computers scale exponentially.

To describe two qubits together you take the tensor (Kronecker) product of their individual state vectors. Two 2-entry vectors combine into a single 4-entry vector whose basis states are |00>, |01>, |10>, |11>.

Each added qubit doubles the dimension: 1 qubit is 2 numbers, 2 qubits are 4, 3 qubits are 8, and n qubits need 2^n complex numbers. This exponential growth is the source of quantum computing's potential power and of the difficulty of simulating it classically.
Gates on separate qubits also combine by tensor product. If you apply H to qubit 0 and nothing (I) to qubit 1, the joint gate is H tensor I, a 4x4 matrix.

items: Combine qubit states with the tensor product
n qubits need 2^n amplitudes
Separate gates combine as A tensor B
Exponential growth = quantum scaling

content.text: The tensor product is like listing every combination on a menu: 2 starters and 2 mains give 4 full meals, 3 and 3 give 9, and so on.

modules.title: From transistors to bits

content.text: The classical bit is the baseline against which the qubit is defined. Understanding what a bit can and cannot do makes the power of the qubit obvious.

A classical bit is the smallest unit of information and holds exactly one of two values, 0 or 1, at any moment. Everything a normal computer does -- numbers, text, images -- is ultimately stored as patterns of bits.
Binary is base-2 counting: each position is a power of two, so 101 in binary is 1*4 + 0*2 + 1*1 = 5. n bits can represent one of 2^n distinct values, but only one value at a time.
The crucial limitation is definiteness: a classical bit is never in between. A qubit, by contrast, can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 at once, which is the first step toward quantum advantage.

items: A bit is 0 or 1, one value at a time
n bits represent 2^n values, but only one at once
Binary place values are powers of 2
A qubit generalises the bit with superposition

content.text: A bit is like a light switch: strictly on or off. A qubit is like a dimmer that can also be set to a blend -- until you look, when it snaps to on or off.
Three bits can encode the numbers 0 through 7 (2^3 = 8 values): 000=0, 001=1, 010=2, ... 111=7, but the register holds only one of these at any instant.

items: Thinking a qubit is just a bit that is sometimes 0 and sometimes 1 -- it is genuinely both until measured.

modules.title: Bytes and data representation

content.text: The four Bell states are the maximally entangled two-qubit states. They are the building blocks of entanglement-based protocols like teleportation and superdense coding.
There are four Bell states: (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt2 and (|01>-|10>)/sqrt2. Together they form an orthonormal basis for the two-qubit space, called the Bell basis.
You create the first Bell state with a Hadamard on the control followed by a CNOT. The other three come from first applying X or Z to one qubit, which flips the bit pattern or the sign.

A Bell measurement projects two qubits onto this basis and is the core operation in teleportation and entanglement swapping. Distinguishing the four Bell states is exactly how the receiver decodes information in superdense coding.

items: Four Bell states form the Bell basis
Built from H then CNOT (plus optional X/Z)
Maximally entangled two-qubit states
Bell measurement underlies teleportation
Superdense coding uses the four states to send 2 bits

content.text: The four Bell states are like four perfectly matched pairs of gloves -- knowing which pair you hold tells you everything about both gloves at once.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                # Phi+ Bell state
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
Starting from |10> (apply X to q0 first), H then CNOT produces (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, the Phi-minus Bell state -- same correlations as Phi-plus but with a relative minus sign.

items: Mixing up which input basis state maps to which Bell state.

modules.title: Boolean logic: XOR

content.text: Classical logic gates combine bits according to fixed rules. Comparing them with quantum gates highlights two differences: reversibility and superposition.

Logic gates take one or more input bits and produce an output bit. AND outputs 1 only when both inputs are 1; OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1; NOT flips a bit; XOR outputs 1 when the inputs differ. A truth table lists every input combination and its output.

Many classical gates are irreversible: knowing that an AND gate output 0 does not tell you the inputs, so information is lost. Quantum gates must be reversible (unitary), which is why the reversible Toffoli gate is used to mimic AND on a quantum computer.
NAND (NOT-AND) is universal classically: any classical circuit can be built from NAND gates alone. Quantum computing has its own universal gate sets, such as {H, T, CNOT}.

items: AND = 1 only if both inputs 1
OR = 1 if any input 1; XOR = 1 if inputs differ
Many classical gates are irreversible (lose information)
Quantum gates must be reversible
NAND is classically universal

content.text: Logic gates are like simple decision rules: AND is 'both must agree', OR is 'at least one', XOR is 'they must differ'.
XOR of 1 and 1 is 0 because the inputs are the same. This same XOR behaviour appears in the quantum CNOT gate, where the target becomes target XOR control.

modules.title: Limits of classical bits

content.text: The classical bit is the baseline against which the qubit is defined. Understanding what a bit can and cannot do makes the power of the qubit obvious.

A classical bit is the smallest unit of information and holds exactly one of two values, 0 or 1, at any moment. Everything a normal computer does -- numbers, text, images -- is ultimately stored as patterns of bits.
Binary is base-2 counting: each position is a power of two, so 101 in binary is 1*4 + 0*2 + 1*1 = 5. n bits can represent one of 2^n distinct values, but only one value at a time.
The crucial limitation is definiteness: a classical bit is never in between. A qubit, by contrast, can be in a superposition of 0 and 1 at once, which is the first step toward quantum advantage.

items: A bit is 0 or 1, one value at a time
n bits represent 2^n values, but only one at once
Binary place values are powers of 2
A qubit generalises the bit with superposition

content.text: A bit is like a light switch: strictly on or off. A qubit is like a dimmer that can also be set to a blend -- until you look, when it snaps to on or off.
Three bits can encode the numbers 0 through 7 (2^3 = 8 values): 000=0, 001=1, 010=2, ... 111=7, but the register holds only one of these at any instant.

items: Thinking a qubit is just a bit that is sometimes 0 and sometimes 1 -- it is genuinely both until measured.

modules.title: Classical registers and memory

content.text: Rotation gates turn a qubit by an arbitrary angle about an axis of the Bloch sphere. They generalise the fixed Pauli gates and build any single-qubit operation.

RX(theta), RY(theta) and RZ(theta) rotate the Bloch-sphere state by angle theta about the X, Y and Z axes respectively. The fixed gates are special cases: X = RX(pi) up to a phase, and Z relates to RZ(pi).

RY(theta) is especially handy because it keeps amplitudes real: RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>, letting you dial any desired split between 0 and 1. RZ changes only the relative phase.

Any single-qubit gate can be written as a product of rotations, for example using the U(theta, phi, lambda) gate with three angles. This is the basis of how compilers express arbitrary operations with hardware-native rotations.

items: RX, RY, RZ rotate by any angle about X, Y, Z
Angles are in radians
RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>
RZ changes relative phase only
Any 1-qubit gate = product of rotations

content.text: Rotation gates are like steering a ball on a globe by a precise number of degrees, rather than only flipping it to the opposite pole.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
import numpy as np
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.ry(np.pi/3, 0)   # 60-degree rotation about Y
qc.measure(0, 0)    # P(1) = sin^2(30deg) = 0.25
RY(pi/2) on |0> gives cos(45deg)|0> + sin(45deg)|1> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 = |+>, so a 90-degree Y-rotation reproduces the Hadamard's superposition (up to phase).

items: Supplying the angle in degrees instead of radians.
Forgetting the half-angle in the cos/sin amplitudes.

modules.title: What is a qubit

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

items: Thinking the qubit secretly already is 0 or 1 before measurement -- superposition is physically real.

modules.title: Superposition: alpha|0> + beta|1>

content.text: Superposition is the ability of a qubit to be in a combination of |0> and |1> simultaneously. It is the first of the two great quantum resources, alongside entanglement.

Superposition means a qubit's state is a weighted sum of basis states, such as (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2. The weights are amplitudes, and the squared magnitudes give the measurement probabilities. The equal superposition |+> gives 50/50 outcomes.

You create superposition with the Hadamard gate. The power comes when many qubits are each in superposition: n qubits can represent all 2^n basis states at once, and a quantum algorithm processes this huge superposition in parallel through interference.

Superposition alone is not magic -- if you just measure, you get one random answer. The art of quantum algorithms is to use interference so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer is amplified before you measure.

items: Superposition = weighted sum of basis states
Created by the Hadamard gate
n qubits hold 2^n basis states at once
Interference turns superposition into useful answers

content.text: Superposition is like a struck bell ringing many notes at once; interference is tuning them so only the note you want is loud when you listen.

H
|0> ---[H]--- (|0> + |1>)/sqrt2   <- equal superposition

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.h([0,1,2])   # all three qubits in superposition -> 8 states at once
qc.measure(range(3), range(3))
After H on |0>, the state is (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2. Over 1000 shots you expect roughly 500 zeros and 500 ones, confirming the equal superposition.

modules.title: State vectors in QVANTA

content.text: A quantum state is a vector. Learning to read, add and normalise vectors lets you treat any qubit state as a concrete list of numbers you can compute with.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, often written as a column. A single qubit lives in a two-dimensional complex vector space, so its state is a column of two complex numbers [alpha, beta], meaning alpha|0> + beta|1>.
You add vectors component by component and scale them by multiplying every entry by a number. Superposition is literally vector addition: |+> = (1/sqrt2)([1,0] + [0,1]) = [1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2].
The length (norm) of a state vector must be 1. For [alpha, beta] this means |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1, which is the normalisation condition guaranteeing the probabilities add to one.

items: A qubit state is a 2-entry complex vector [alpha, beta]
Add vectors entrywise; scale by a scalar
Norm must equal 1: |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1

content.text: A state vector is like a recipe: each entry is how much of each basis ingredient (|0> and |1>) to mix in.
The state 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> is the vector [0.6, 0.8]. Check the norm: 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, so it is a valid state. Measuring gives 0 with probability 0.36 and 1 with probability 0.64.

items: Using an un-normalised vector -- always check the entries squared add to 1.

modules.title: Pure vs mixed states intuition

content.text: The density matrix generalises the state vector to describe mixed states and noisy, open systems. It is the right tool whenever you have classical uncertainty or entanglement with an environment.

A pure state can be written as a vector, but a statistical mixture of states (classical uncertainty) cannot. The density matrix rho captures both pure and mixed states as a positive matrix with trace 1. A pure state has rho = |psi><psi| and satisfies rho^2 = rho.

When two qubits are entangled, each one alone is described by a mixed density matrix obtained by the partial trace over the other. This is how entanglement looks from a single-qubit viewpoint: more entanglement means a more mixed local state.

Noise and open-system dynamics are described by quantum channels acting on density matrices, often written in Kraus or Lindblad form. This formalism underlies realistic hardware modelling and error correction.

items: rho describes pure and mixed states alike
rho is positive with trace 1; pure means rho^2 = rho
Partial trace gives the state of a subsystem
Entangled qubits have mixed local density matrices
Noise = quantum channels acting on rho

content.text: A state vector is a sharp photograph; a density matrix is a photograph that may be blurred by classical uncertainty or by entanglement with things outside the frame.

pure:  rho = |psi><psi|,  rho^2 = rho
mixed: rho = sum_i p_i |psi_i><psi_i|,  rho^2 != rho
For the Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, tracing out the second qubit leaves the first in rho = (|0><0| + |1><1|)/2, a maximally mixed state -- the hallmark of maximal entanglement.

items: Trying to describe a subsystem of an entangled pair with a state vector -- you must use the (mixed) density matrix.

modules.title: Qubit vs classical bit side by side

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

modules.title: Introducing the Bloch sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is a picture that turns any single-qubit state into a point on a sphere, making superposition and gates visually intuitive.

Every pure single-qubit state maps to a point on the surface of a unit sphere. The north pole is |0>, the south pole is |1>, and points on the equator are equal superpositions such as |+>, |->, |+i> and |-i>.

A state is fixed by two angles: theta, the polar angle from the north pole, and phi, the azimuthal angle around the equator. The state is cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi) sin(theta/2)|1>. The angle phi is the relative phase.

Single-qubit gates are rotations of this sphere. X, Y and Z are 180-degree rotations about their axes; the rotation gates rx, ry, rz turn by any angle. This is why visualising gates as rotations is so powerful.

items: North pole = |0>, south pole = |1>
Equator = equal superpositions
Angles theta (polar) and phi (phase) fix the state
Gates are rotations of the sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is like a globe where your qubit is a pin; gates spin the globe to move the pin to a new latitude and longitude.
The state |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 sits on the equator at phi = 0 (theta = 90 degrees). Applying Z moves it to |-> on the opposite side of the equator (phi = 180 degrees).

modules.title: The equator and superposition states

content.text: Superposition is the ability of a qubit to be in a combination of |0> and |1> simultaneously. It is the first of the two great quantum resources, alongside entanglement.

Superposition means a qubit's state is a weighted sum of basis states, such as (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2. The weights are amplitudes, and the squared magnitudes give the measurement probabilities. The equal superposition |+> gives 50/50 outcomes.

You create superposition with the Hadamard gate. The power comes when many qubits are each in superposition: n qubits can represent all 2^n basis states at once, and a quantum algorithm processes this huge superposition in parallel through interference.

Superposition alone is not magic -- if you just measure, you get one random answer. The art of quantum algorithms is to use interference so that wrong answers cancel and the right answer is amplified before you measure.

items: Superposition = weighted sum of basis states
Created by the Hadamard gate
n qubits hold 2^n basis states at once
Interference turns superposition into useful answers

content.text: Superposition is like a struck bell ringing many notes at once; interference is tuning them so only the note you want is loud when you listen.

H
|0> ---[H]--- (|0> + |1>)/sqrt2   <- equal superposition

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.h([0,1,2])   # all three qubits in superposition -> 8 states at once
qc.measure(range(3), range(3))
After H on |0>, the state is (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2. Over 1000 shots you expect roughly 500 zeros and 500 ones, confirming the equal superposition.

items: Believing superposition by itself gives a speed-up -- you also need interference and clever algorithm design.

modules.title: Gates as rotations on the Bloch sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is a picture that turns any single-qubit state into a point on a sphere, making superposition and gates visually intuitive.

Every pure single-qubit state maps to a point on the surface of a unit sphere. The north pole is |0>, the south pole is |1>, and points on the equator are equal superpositions such as |+>, |->, |+i> and |-i>.

A state is fixed by two angles: theta, the polar angle from the north pole, and phi, the azimuthal angle around the equator. The state is cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi) sin(theta/2)|1>. The angle phi is the relative phase.

Single-qubit gates are rotations of this sphere. X, Y and Z are 180-degree rotations about their axes; the rotation gates rx, ry, rz turn by any angle. This is why visualising gates as rotations is so powerful.

items: North pole = |0>, south pole = |1>
Equator = equal superpositions
Angles theta (polar) and phi (phase) fix the state
Gates are rotations of the sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is like a globe where your qubit is a pin; gates spin the globe to move the pin to a new latitude and longitude.
The state |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 sits on the equator at phi = 0 (theta = 90 degrees). Applying Z moves it to |-> on the opposite side of the equator (phi = 180 degrees).

modules.title: Gates as unitary matrices

content.text: Matrices are how quantum gates are written, and matrix multiplication is how a gate acts on a state. Master this and every gate becomes a concrete calculation.

A matrix is a rectangular grid of numbers. A single-qubit gate is a 2x2 complex matrix; an n-qubit gate is a 2^n by 2^n matrix. Applying a gate to a state means multiplying the gate matrix by the state vector.

To multiply a 2x2 matrix by a 2-entry vector, each output entry is the dot product of a matrix row with the vector. Order matters: gates applied later sit to the left in the product, so the circuit G2 then G1 is written G1*G2 as matrices.
Matrix multiplication is associative but generally not commutative: A*B is usually different from B*A. This non-commuting behaviour is why the order of quantum gates changes the result.

items: Single-qubit gate = 2x2 matrix; n qubits = 2^n size
Apply a gate = matrix times state vector
Each output entry is a row-times-vector dot product
Matrix multiplication is not commutative
Later gate sits left in the matrix product

content.text: A matrix is a machine that takes a vector in and gives a transformed vector out; multiplying matrices is like chaining machines on a conveyor belt.

[ a b ] [ x ]   [ a*x + b*y ]
[ c d ] [ y ] = [ c*x + d*y ]
Apply X = [[0,1],[1,0]] to |0> = [1,0]: top entry = 0*1 + 1*0 = 0; bottom entry = 1*1 + 0*0 = 1. Result [0,1] = |1>, confirming X flips |0> to |1>.

modules.title: The identity gate

content.text: This module explains the Identity (I) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The identity gate does nothing to the quantum state: I|psi> = |psi>. Although that sounds useless, it is important as a placeholder for timing, for keeping circuit diagrams aligned, and as the neutral element in gate algebra (G*I = I*G = G).
In noise modelling, an identity 'gate' still takes time on real hardware, so even doing nothing exposes the qubit to decoherence -- a subtle but important point when you reason about T1 and T2.

modules.title: The Pauli-X (NOT / bit-flip) gate

content.text: This module explains the Pauli-X (NOT / bit-flip) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Pauli-X gate is the quantum version of the classical NOT gate. It flips the computational basis states: it turns |0> into |1> and |1> into |0>. For a general qubit alpha|0> + beta|1>, it swaps the two amplitudes, giving beta|0> + alpha|1>.
Geometrically, X is a 180-degree rotation of the Bloch sphere about the X-axis. The north pole (|0>) and south pole (|1>) swap places, which is exactly why it behaves like a bit-flip.

X is both Hermitian (equal to its own conjugate transpose) and unitary, and it is its own inverse: applying X twice returns the original state because X*X = I. This makes it a very safe gate to experiment with.
Action: X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
On the Bloch sphere: 180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

items: Symbol: X
X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.x(0)            # bit-flip: |0> -> |1>
qc.measure(0, 0)   # you will measure 1 with certainty
Now take 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> = [0.6, 0.8]. After X we get [0.8, 0.6] = 0.8|0> + 0.6|1>: the measurement probabilities 0 and 1 have swapped from 0.36/0.64 to 0.64/0.36.

modules.title: The Pauli-Y gate

content.text: This module explains the Pauli-Y gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Pauli-Y gate performs a bit-flip and a phase-flip at the same time. Acting on the basis states it gives Y|0> = i|1> and Y|1> = -i|0>, so it both swaps the amplitudes and multiplies them by factors of +/- i.
Algebraically Y = i*X*Z, which is why it combines the effects of the X (bit-flip) and Z (phase-flip) gates. On the Bloch sphere it is a 180-degree rotation about the Y-axis.
Like the other Pauli gates, Y is Hermitian and unitary and is its own inverse (Y*Y = I). It appears constantly in error-correction (Y-type errors) and in rotation decompositions.
Action: Y|0> = i|1>, Y|1> = -i|0> (bit-flip plus phase).
On the Bloch sphere: 180-degree rotation about the Bloch Y-axis.

Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.

modules.title: The Pauli-Z (phase-flip) gate

content.text: This module explains the Pauli-Z (phase-flip) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The Pauli-Z gate leaves |0> unchanged and multiplies |1> by -1, so Z|0> = |0> and Z|1> = -|1>. It is called a phase-flip because it flips the sign (phase) of the |1> component only.

Importantly, Z does not change the measurement probabilities in the Z (computational) basis, because the magnitude of each amplitude is unchanged. What it changes is the relative phase, which affects interference. To actually see the effect, sandwich Z between two Hadamards.
On the Bloch sphere, Z is a 180-degree rotation about the Z-axis: states on the equator (like |+>) are rotated to the opposite side (|->).
Action: Z|0> = |0>, Z|1> = -|1>; flips the phase of |1>.
On the Bloch sphere: 180-degree rotation about the Bloch Z-axis.

items: Symbol: Z
Z|0> = |0>, Z|1> = -|1>; flips the phase of |1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.

modules.title: The Hadamard gate H

content.text: This module explains the Hadamard (H) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Hadamard gate is the single most important gate in quantum computing because it creates superposition. It maps |0> to |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 and |1> to |-> = (|0>-|1>)/sqrt2, turning a definite state into an equal mixture of 0 and 1.

If you measure a qubit right after a Hadamard, you get 0 and 1 each with 50 percent probability. This is the starting move of almost every quantum algorithm -- Deutsch-Jozsa, Grover, Shor and QFT all begin by spreading the input into superposition with Hadamards.

Hadamard is its own inverse (H*H = I), so two Hadamards cancel. On the Bloch sphere it rotates the Z-axis onto the X-axis, which is why it also acts as a change of basis between the Z and X measurement bases.
On the Bloch sphere: Maps |0> (north pole) to |+> on the equator; swaps the Z and X axes.

modules.title: The S (phase) gate

content.text: This module explains the S (phase) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The S gate adds a 90-degree (quarter-turn) phase to the |1> component: it leaves |0> alone and multiplies |1> by i. Because applying it twice gives Z, we say S is the square root of Z (S*S = Z).
On the Bloch sphere it is a +90-degree rotation about the Z-axis, so it moves states around the equator. Its inverse is the S-dagger gate, which applies -90 degrees instead.
S belongs to the Clifford group, the set of gates that can be simulated efficiently on a classical computer. On its own the Clifford group is not universal -- you also need the T gate.
Action: S|0> = |0>, S|1> = i|1>; a 90-degree phase on |1>.
On the Bloch sphere: +90-degree rotation about the Z-axis.

items: Symbol: S
S|0> = |0>, S|1> = i|1>; a 90-degree phase on |1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
+90-degree rotation about the Z-axis.

modules.title: The T gate

content.text: This module explains the T gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The T gate adds a 45-degree phase to the |1> component. It is the square root of S (T*T = S), and two S gates give Z, so four T gates give Z.
The T gate is crucial because it is non-Clifford: adding T to the Clifford gates {H, S, CNOT} makes a universal gate set, meaning you can approximate any quantum operation to arbitrary accuracy.

In fault-tolerant quantum computing, T gates are expensive. They cannot be done transversally in most codes and are produced through a costly process called magic-state distillation, so algorithm designers try to minimise the 'T-count'.
Action: T|1> = e^(i*pi/4)|1>; a 45-degree phase on |1>.
On the Bloch sphere: +45-degree rotation about the Z-axis.

items: Symbol: T
T|1> = e^(i*pi/4)|1>; a 45-degree phase on |1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
+45-degree rotation about the Z-axis.

qc.t(0)
qc.tdg(0)   # T-dagger (inverse)

modules.title: Rotation gate Rx(theta)

content.text: Rotation gates turn a qubit by an arbitrary angle about an axis of the Bloch sphere. They generalise the fixed Pauli gates and build any single-qubit operation.

RX(theta), RY(theta) and RZ(theta) rotate the Bloch-sphere state by angle theta about the X, Y and Z axes respectively. The fixed gates are special cases: X = RX(pi) up to a phase, and Z relates to RZ(pi).

RY(theta) is especially handy because it keeps amplitudes real: RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>, letting you dial any desired split between 0 and 1. RZ changes only the relative phase.

Any single-qubit gate can be written as a product of rotations, for example using the U(theta, phi, lambda) gate with three angles. This is the basis of how compilers express arbitrary operations with hardware-native rotations.

items: RX, RY, RZ rotate by any angle about X, Y, Z
Angles are in radians
RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>
RZ changes relative phase only
Any 1-qubit gate = product of rotations

content.text: Rotation gates are like steering a ball on a globe by a precise number of degrees, rather than only flipping it to the opposite pole.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
import numpy as np
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.ry(np.pi/3, 0)   # 60-degree rotation about Y
qc.measure(0, 0)    # P(1) = sin^2(30deg) = 0.25
RY(pi/2) on |0> gives cos(45deg)|0> + sin(45deg)|1> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 = |+>, so a 90-degree Y-rotation reproduces the Hadamard's superposition (up to phase).

modules.title: Composing single-qubit gates

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /

modules.title: Sequences on the Bloch sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is a picture that turns any single-qubit state into a point on a sphere, making superposition and gates visually intuitive.

Every pure single-qubit state maps to a point on the surface of a unit sphere. The north pole is |0>, the south pole is |1>, and points on the equator are equal superpositions such as |+>, |->, |+i> and |-i>.

A state is fixed by two angles: theta, the polar angle from the north pole, and phi, the azimuthal angle around the equator. The state is cos(theta/2)|0> + e^(i*phi) sin(theta/2)|1>. The angle phi is the relative phase.

Single-qubit gates are rotations of this sphere. X, Y and Z are 180-degree rotations about their axes; the rotation gates rx, ry, rz turn by any angle. This is why visualising gates as rotations is so powerful.

items: North pole = |0>, south pole = |1>
Equator = equal superpositions
Angles theta (polar) and phi (phase) fix the state
Gates are rotations of the sphere

content.text: The Bloch sphere is like a globe where your qubit is a pin; gates spin the globe to move the pin to a new latitude and longitude.
The state |+> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 sits on the equator at phi = 0 (theta = 90 degrees). Applying Z moves it to |-> on the opposite side of the equator (phi = 180 degrees).

modules.title: What measurement does to a qubit

content.text: Measurement is how a quantum state becomes a classical result. It is probabilistic, irreversible, and the only non-unitary step in a quantum circuit.

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, you get 0 or 1 with probabilities given by the Born rule (|amplitude|^2). The act of measuring collapses the state onto the outcome you saw: after measuring 1, the qubit is now exactly |1>.

Collapse is irreversible and destroys the superposition, so you cannot read the amplitudes directly. To learn the distribution you prepare and measure the same circuit many times (shots) and build a histogram of outcomes.
You can measure in other bases too. Measuring in the X basis is done by applying a Hadamard first and then measuring in the Z basis, which is how you probe phase information that the Z basis hides.

items: Outcome probability = |amplitude|^2
Measurement collapses the state onto the result
It is irreversible and destroys superposition
Repeat many shots to see the distribution
Change basis by rotating before measuring

content.text: Measurement is like opening a wrapped gift: before opening, several possibilities exist; opening fixes one and you cannot un-open it.

(|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 --[measure]--> 0  (state now |0>)
                           or  1  (state now |1>)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)
result = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())   # about {'0': 500, '1': 500}
Measuring |+> once might give 0; the qubit then collapses to |0>, and measuring again immediately gives 0 with certainty. The randomness was in the first measurement only.

modules.title: Born rule: probabilities from amplitudes

content.text: Measurement outcomes are random, and the Born rule tells you their probabilities. This is the bridge from a quantum state to the histogram the simulator shows you.

The Born rule states that the probability of measuring a particular basis outcome equals the squared magnitude of that outcome's amplitude. For alpha|0> + beta|1>, you get 0 with probability |alpha|^2 and 1 with probability |beta|^2.

Because the state is normalised, these probabilities add to 1. A single measurement gives one random outcome and collapses the state; to see the full distribution you run many shots and build a histogram.
The expectation value is the average outcome weighted by probability. For an observable it is computed as <psi|A|psi> and is what many algorithms, such as VQE, actually try to minimise.

items: Probability = |amplitude|^2 (Born rule)
Probabilities add to 1
One shot gives one random outcome and collapses the state
Many shots build a histogram
Expectation value = <psi|A|psi>

content.text: A quantum state is like a weighted dice: the amplitudes squared are the chances of each face, and each roll (shot) gives just one face.

state: alpha|0> + beta|1>

P(0) = |alpha|^2
P(1) = |beta|^2
P(0) + P(1) = 1
For (|0> + i|1>)/sqrt2, alpha = 1/sqrt2 and beta = i/sqrt2. P(0) = |1/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5 and P(1) = |i/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5, so the histogram over many shots is about half 0 and half 1.

items: Using the amplitude itself instead of its squared magnitude for the probability.
Forgetting that a phase like i does not change a single-measurement probability.

modules.title: Measurement is irreversible

content.text: Measurement is how a quantum state becomes a classical result. It is probabilistic, irreversible, and the only non-unitary step in a quantum circuit.

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, you get 0 or 1 with probabilities given by the Born rule (|amplitude|^2). The act of measuring collapses the state onto the outcome you saw: after measuring 1, the qubit is now exactly |1>.

Collapse is irreversible and destroys the superposition, so you cannot read the amplitudes directly. To learn the distribution you prepare and measure the same circuit many times (shots) and build a histogram of outcomes.
You can measure in other bases too. Measuring in the X basis is done by applying a Hadamard first and then measuring in the Z basis, which is how you probe phase information that the Z basis hides.

modules.title: From one qubit to two

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

modules.title: Tensor products of qubit states

content.text: The tensor product is how the states of separate qubits combine into one joint state. It is the reason quantum computers scale exponentially.

To describe two qubits together you take the tensor (Kronecker) product of their individual state vectors. Two 2-entry vectors combine into a single 4-entry vector whose basis states are |00>, |01>, |10>, |11>.

Each added qubit doubles the dimension: 1 qubit is 2 numbers, 2 qubits are 4, 3 qubits are 8, and n qubits need 2^n complex numbers. This exponential growth is the source of quantum computing's potential power and of the difficulty of simulating it classically.
Gates on separate qubits also combine by tensor product. If you apply H to qubit 0 and nothing (I) to qubit 1, the joint gate is H tensor I, a 4x4 matrix.

items: Combine qubit states with the tensor product
n qubits need 2^n amplitudes
Separate gates combine as A tensor B
Exponential growth = quantum scaling

content.text: The tensor product is like listing every combination on a menu: 2 starters and 2 mains give 4 full meals, 3 and 3 give 9, and so on.
|0> tensor |1> = [1,0] tensor [0,1] = [0,1,0,0] = |01>. The single 1 sits in the position labelled 01, confirming the combined state is |01>.

items: Adding the dimensions (2+2) instead of multiplying them (2*2=4).

modules.title: Introducing entanglement

content.text: Entanglement is a uniquely quantum correlation between qubits that is stronger than anything classical. It is the key resource behind teleportation, cryptography and quantum speed-ups.

Two qubits are entangled when their joint state cannot be written as a tensor product of two separate single-qubit states. The Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2 is the simplest example: there is no way to assign a definite individual state to each qubit.

Measuring one entangled qubit instantly determines the correlated outcome of the other, no matter how far apart they are. In the Bell state, if you measure the first qubit as 0 the second is guaranteed 0, and if 1 then 1. The outcomes are perfectly correlated yet individually random.

Entanglement does not allow faster-than-light signalling, because each local result still looks random; the correlation only shows up when the two parties compare notes. But as a computational resource it lets quantum algorithms explore correlations no classical machine can efficiently reproduce.

items: Entangled state cannot be factored into separate qubit states
Measuring one qubit fixes the other's correlated outcome
Outcomes are individually random but perfectly correlated
No faster-than-light signalling
A core resource for teleportation and speed-ups

content.text: Entanglement is like two magic coins that always land the same way as each other, even in different cities -- each looks random alone, but compared they match perfectly.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                # create entanglement
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])   # only 00 and 11 appear
Build (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2 and run 1000 shots: you see roughly 500 '00' and 500 '11', and never '01' or '10' -- the signature of entanglement.

modules.title: The Bell state |Phi+>

content.text: The four Bell states are the maximally entangled two-qubit states. They are the building blocks of entanglement-based protocols like teleportation and superdense coding.
There are four Bell states: (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt2 and (|01>-|10>)/sqrt2. Together they form an orthonormal basis for the two-qubit space, called the Bell basis.
You create the first Bell state with a Hadamard on the control followed by a CNOT. The other three come from first applying X or Z to one qubit, which flips the bit pattern or the sign.

A Bell measurement projects two qubits onto this basis and is the core operation in teleportation and entanglement swapping. Distinguishing the four Bell states is exactly how the receiver decodes information in superdense coding.

items: Four Bell states form the Bell basis
Built from H then CNOT (plus optional X/Z)
Maximally entangled two-qubit states
Bell measurement underlies teleportation
Superdense coding uses the four states to send 2 bits

content.text: The four Bell states are like four perfectly matched pairs of gloves -- knowing which pair you hold tells you everything about both gloves at once.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                # Phi+ Bell state
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
Starting from |10> (apply X to q0 first), H then CNOT produces (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, the Phi-minus Bell state -- same correlations as Phi-plus but with a relative minus sign.

modules.title: Three-qubit states

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

modules.title: GHZ and W states intuition

content.text: The GHZ state is a three-or-more-qubit maximally entangled state. It generalises the Bell state and reveals even sharper non-classical behaviour.
The three-qubit GHZ state is (|000>+|111>)/sqrt2. All qubits are either all 0 or all 1, perfectly correlated. You build it with a Hadamard on the first qubit followed by a chain of CNOTs.

GHZ states show 'all-or-nothing' entanglement: measuring any one qubit instantly fixes all the others. They are used in multiparty protocols, quantum secret sharing and in dramatic tests of quantum mechanics that rule out local hidden-variable theories without needing statistics.
GHZ entanglement is also fragile: losing a single qubit destroys the entanglement of the whole state, which contrasts with more robust states like the W state.

items: GHZ: (|000>+|111>)/sqrt2 for 3 qubits
Built from H then a chain of CNOTs
All qubits perfectly correlated (all 0 or all 1)
Used in secret sharing and foundational tests
Fragile: losing one qubit breaks the entanglement

content.text: A GHZ state is like three dancers locked in step: they all step left together or all step right together, never out of sync.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)                   # GHZ state
qc.measure(range(3), range(3))
Run the GHZ circuit for 1000 shots: you see about 500 '000' and 500 '111', and none of the other six outcomes -- confirming all-or-nothing correlation.

modules.title: Reduced states and partial trace intuition

content.text: The density matrix generalises the state vector to describe mixed states and noisy, open systems. It is the right tool whenever you have classical uncertainty or entanglement with an environment.

A pure state can be written as a vector, but a statistical mixture of states (classical uncertainty) cannot. The density matrix rho captures both pure and mixed states as a positive matrix with trace 1. A pure state has rho = |psi><psi| and satisfies rho^2 = rho.

When two qubits are entangled, each one alone is described by a mixed density matrix obtained by the partial trace over the other. This is how entanglement looks from a single-qubit viewpoint: more entanglement means a more mixed local state.

Noise and open-system dynamics are described by quantum channels acting on density matrices, often written in Kraus or Lindblad form. This formalism underlies realistic hardware modelling and error correction.

items: rho describes pure and mixed states alike
rho is positive with trace 1; pure means rho^2 = rho
Partial trace gives the state of a subsystem
Entangled qubits have mixed local density matrices
Noise = quantum channels acting on rho

content.text: A state vector is a sharp photograph; a density matrix is a photograph that may be blurred by classical uncertainty or by entanglement with things outside the frame.

pure:  rho = |psi><psi|,  rho^2 = rho
mixed: rho = sum_i p_i |psi_i><psi_i|,  rho^2 != rho
For the Bell state (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, tracing out the second qubit leaves the first in rho = (|0><0| + |1><1|)/2, a maximally mixed state -- the hallmark of maximal entanglement.

items: Trying to describe a subsystem of an entangled pair with a state vector -- you must use the (mixed) density matrix.

modules.title: The CNOT (CX) gate

content.text: This module explains the Pauli-X (NOT / bit-flip) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Pauli-X gate is the quantum version of the classical NOT gate. It flips the computational basis states: it turns |0> into |1> and |1> into |0>. For a general qubit alpha|0> + beta|1>, it swaps the two amplitudes, giving beta|0> + alpha|1>.
Geometrically, X is a 180-degree rotation of the Bloch sphere about the X-axis. The north pole (|0>) and south pole (|1>) swap places, which is exactly why it behaves like a bit-flip.

X is both Hermitian (equal to its own conjugate transpose) and unitary, and it is its own inverse: applying X twice returns the original state because X*X = I. This makes it a very safe gate to experiment with.
Action: X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
On the Bloch sphere: 180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

items: Symbol: X
X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.x(0)            # bit-flip: |0> -> |1>
qc.measure(0, 0)   # you will measure 1 with certainty
Now take 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> = [0.6, 0.8]. After X we get [0.8, 0.6] = 0.8|0> + 0.6|1>: the measurement probabilities 0 and 1 have swapped from 0.36/0.64 to 0.64/0.36.

modules.title: CNOT truth table

content.text: This module explains the CNOT (controlled-NOT / CX) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The CNOT gate is the fundamental two-qubit gate. It uses one qubit as the control and one as the target: if the control is |1> it applies an X (flip) to the target, and if the control is |0> it does nothing. In formula form, target becomes (target XOR control).
CNOT is the key to building entanglement. Put the control into superposition with a Hadamard first, then apply CNOT, and you create a Bell state in which the two qubits are perfectly correlated.
On basis states it maps |00>->|00>, |01>->|01>, |10>->|11>, |11>->|10>. It is reversible (its own inverse) and is one of the native two-qubit gates on most real hardware.
Action: If control = 1, flip the target; target -> target XOR control.
On the Bloch sphere: Two-qubit gate; cannot be shown on a single Bloch sphere.

items: Symbol: CX
If control = 1, flip the target; target -> target XOR control.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
Two-qubit gate; cannot be shown on a single Bloch sphere.

content.text: Picture this idea as one clear step that builds directly on the previous module.

qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                 # control 0, target 1 -> Bell state
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])    # about 50% 00, 50% 11
Apply H to qubit 0 to get (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 on the control, then CNOT with target qubit 1. The joint state becomes (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, the Bell state -- measuring always gives 00 or 11, never 01 or 10.

modules.title: The controlled-Z (CZ) gate

content.text: This module explains the Controlled-Z (CZ) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The controlled-Z gate applies a Z (phase flip) to the target only when the control is |1>. In practice it just multiplies the |11> component by -1 and leaves the other three basis states unchanged.

Unlike CNOT, CZ is symmetric: it does not matter which qubit you call the control and which the target, the result is the same. You can build CZ from a CNOT by surrounding the target with Hadamards: CZ = H(target) * CNOT * H(target).
CZ is the natural entangling gate for cluster states and graph states, which are the backbone of measurement-based quantum computing.
Action: Multiplies the |11> amplitude by -1; otherwise unchanged.
On the Bloch sphere: Two-qubit phase gate.

modules.title: The SWAP gate

content.text: This module explains the SWAP gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The SWAP gate exchanges the full quantum states of two qubits, so |01> becomes |10> and vice versa. The |00> and |11> states are unchanged.
SWAP can be built from three CNOTs: CX(a,b) then CX(b,a) then CX(a,b). This matters because real hardware rarely has a native SWAP, and swapping costs three two-qubit gates.
SWAPs are inserted automatically by the transpiler to move logical qubits next to each other when the hardware has limited connectivity, so understanding SWAP helps you reason about circuit overhead.
Action: Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
On the Bloch sphere: Two-qubit gate.

items: Symbol: SWAP
Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.

modules.title: Decomposing Toffoli into basic gates

content.text: This module explains the Toffoli (CCX) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Toffoli, or controlled-controlled-NOT (CCX), gate has two control qubits and one target. It flips the target only when both controls are |1>. This makes it a reversible version of the classical AND gate.

Because it is reversible and can reproduce AND and NAND behaviour, the Toffoli gate is classically universal: any classical circuit can be rebuilt from Toffoli gates with the help of extra ancilla qubits.

Hardware cannot run a three-qubit gate directly, so Toffoli is decomposed into about six CNOTs plus several single-qubit T, T-dagger and H gates. It appears everywhere in quantum arithmetic and error correction.
