modules.title: Universal gate sets

content.text: Shor's algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA encryption. It reduces factoring to period-finding, which a quantum computer solves efficiently with the QFT.

To factor N, Shor picks a random a coprime to N and looks for the period r of the function f(x) = a^x mod N, meaning the smallest r with a^r = 1 mod N. Finding r is the hard part classically, but easy quantumly.

The quantum core prepares a superposition over x, computes a^x mod N into a second register, and applies the QFT to extract the period r via phase estimation. Once r is known (and is even, with a^(r/2) not equal to -1 mod N), the factors come from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N).

Because the best known classical factoring algorithms are sub-exponential while Shor is polynomial, a large fault-tolerant quantum computer could break RSA and related public-key cryptography. This is the main driver of post-quantum cryptography.

Reduces factoring to finding the period of a^x mod N
Quantum period-finding uses the QFT
Factors from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N)
Breaks RSA, driving post-quantum cryptography

For N = 15 with a = 7, the period of 7^x mod 15 is r = 4. Then gcd(7^2 - 1, 15) = gcd(48,15) = 3 and gcd(7^2 + 1, 15) = gcd(50,15) = 5, giving the factors 3 and 5.

modules.title: Anatomy of a quantum circuit

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

modules.title: Qubit rails and time order

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

modules.title: The four Bell states

content.text: The four Bell states are the maximally entangled two-qubit states. They are the building blocks of entanglement-based protocols like teleportation and superdense coding.
There are four Bell states: (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt2 and (|01>-|10>)/sqrt2. Together they form an orthonormal basis for the two-qubit space, called the Bell basis.
You create the first Bell state with a Hadamard on the control followed by a CNOT. The other three come from first applying X or Z to one qubit, which flips the bit pattern or the sign.

A Bell measurement projects two qubits onto this basis and is the core operation in teleportation and entanglement swapping. Distinguishing the four Bell states is exactly how the receiver decodes information in superdense coding.

items: Four Bell states form the Bell basis
Built from H then CNOT (plus optional X/Z)
Maximally entangled two-qubit states
Bell measurement underlies teleportation
Superdense coding uses the four states to send 2 bits

content.text: The four Bell states are like four perfectly matched pairs of gloves -- knowing which pair you hold tells you everything about both gloves at once.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                # Phi+ Bell state
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
Starting from |10> (apply X to q0 first), H then CNOT produces (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, the Phi-minus Bell state -- same correlations as Phi-plus but with a relative minus sign.

modules.title: Superdense coding idea

content.text: Superdense coding is the mirror image of teleportation: it sends two classical bits by transmitting just one qubit, using a shared entangled pair.

Alice and Bob share a Bell pair in advance. To send two classical bits, Alice applies one of four operations (I, X, Z or ZX) to her single qubit, which rotates the shared pair into one of the four distinct Bell states.
Alice sends her one qubit to Bob. Bob now holds both halves of the pair and performs a Bell measurement, which distinguishes the four Bell states and recovers the two classical bits Alice chose.

The pre-shared entanglement is what doubles the capacity: one physical qubit carries two classical bits of information. Without the entanglement, one qubit could reliably carry only one bit (Holevo bound).

items: Sends 2 classical bits using 1 transmitted qubit
Requires a pre-shared Bell pair
Alice encodes with I, X, Z or ZX
Bob decodes with a Bell measurement
Entanglement doubles the channel capacity

content.text: Superdense coding is like agreeing on a secret codebook (the entangled pair) beforehand, so one short word later conveys a longer message.

encode (Alice, choose op):
00 -> I   01 -> X
10 -> Z   11 -> ZX

Alice sends 1 qubit -> Bob does Bell measurement -> 2 bits

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1)      # shared Bell pair
# Alice encodes '11':
qc.z(0); qc.x(0)
# Bob decodes:
qc.cx(0, 1); qc.h(0)
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
To send bits '10', Alice applies Z only. Bob's Bell measurement then reads out '10' with certainty.

modules.title: Quantum teleportation overview

content.text: Quantum teleportation transfers an unknown qubit state from one place to another using a shared entangled pair plus two classical bits -- without moving the qubit itself.

The sender (Alice) and receiver (Bob) first share a Bell pair. Alice has the unknown state |psi> she wants to send. She performs a Bell measurement on |psi> and her half of the pair, getting two classical bits as the result.

Alice sends those two classical bits to Bob over an ordinary channel. Depending on the two bits, Bob applies one of four corrections (I, X, Z or ZX) to his half of the pair, which then becomes exactly |psi>.

No faster-than-light communication happens, because Bob's qubit is useless until the classical bits arrive. The original |psi> is destroyed by Alice's measurement, consistent with the no-cloning theorem -- teleportation moves a state, it does not copy it.

items: Needs a shared Bell pair plus 2 classical bits
Alice does a Bell measurement, sends 2 bits
Bob applies I, X, Z or ZX to recover |psi>
No faster-than-light signalling (classical bits required)
Original state is destroyed (no cloning)

content.text: Teleportation is like faxing a sculpture: the original is consumed to extract instructions, which are sent so an identical one is rebuilt at the other end.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
# q0 = state to send, q1-q2 = Bell pair
qc.h(1); qc.cx(1, 2)
qc.cx(0, 1); qc.h(0)
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
qc.cx(1, 2); qc.cz(0, 2)   # Bob's corrections
If Alice's Bell measurement gives bits 1 and 0, Bob applies an X correction; if it gives 1 and 1, he applies both Z and X. Only after the right correction is his qubit guaranteed to equal |psi>.

items: Believing teleportation copies the state or sends it instantly -- it destroys the original and needs classical bits.

modules.title: Entanglement swapping intuition

content.text: This module explains the SWAP gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The SWAP gate exchanges the full quantum states of two qubits, so |01> becomes |10> and vice versa. The |00> and |11> states are unchanged.
SWAP can be built from three CNOTs: CX(a,b) then CX(b,a) then CX(a,b). This matters because real hardware rarely has a native SWAP, and swapping costs three two-qubit gates.
SWAPs are inserted automatically by the transpiler to move logical qubits next to each other when the hardware has limited connectivity, so understanding SWAP helps you reason about circuit overhead.
Action: Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
On the Bloch sphere: Two-qubit gate.

items: Symbol: SWAP
Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
Two-qubit gate.

modules.title: Why Qiskit and Qiskit Aer

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

modules.title: Adding single-qubit gates in code

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

items: Thinking the qubit secretly already is 0 or 1 before measurement -- superposition is physically real.

modules.title: Measurement in code

content.text: Measurement is how a quantum state becomes a classical result. It is probabilistic, irreversible, and the only non-unitary step in a quantum circuit.

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, you get 0 or 1 with probabilities given by the Born rule (|amplitude|^2). The act of measuring collapses the state onto the outcome you saw: after measuring 1, the qubit is now exactly |1>.

Collapse is irreversible and destroys the superposition, so you cannot read the amplitudes directly. To learn the distribution you prepare and measure the same circuit many times (shots) and build a histogram of outcomes.
You can measure in other bases too. Measuring in the X basis is done by applying a Hadamard first and then measuring in the Z basis, which is how you probe phase information that the Z basis hides.

items: Outcome probability = |amplitude|^2
Measurement collapses the state onto the result
It is irreversible and destroys superposition
Repeat many shots to see the distribution
Change basis by rotating before measuring

content.text: Measurement is like opening a wrapped gift: before opening, several possibilities exist; opening fixes one and you cannot un-open it.

(|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 --[measure]--> 0  (state now |0>)
                           or  1  (state now |1>)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)
result = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())   # about {'0': 500, '1': 500}
Measuring |+> once might give 0; the qubit then collapses to |0>, and measuring again immediately gives 0 with certainty. The randomness was in the first measurement only.

items: Expecting a single measurement to reveal the amplitudes -- it only gives one random outcome.

modules.title: Running on the Aer simulator

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

items: Forgetting to add measurements, which leaves get_counts() with nothing to report.

modules.title: Statevector simulation

content.text: A quantum state is a vector. Learning to read, add and normalise vectors lets you treat any qubit state as a concrete list of numbers you can compute with.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers, often written as a column. A single qubit lives in a two-dimensional complex vector space, so its state is a column of two complex numbers [alpha, beta], meaning alpha|0> + beta|1>.
You add vectors component by component and scale them by multiplying every entry by a number. Superposition is literally vector addition: |+> = (1/sqrt2)([1,0] + [0,1]) = [1/sqrt2, 1/sqrt2].
The length (norm) of a state vector must be 1. For [alpha, beta] this means |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1, which is the normalisation condition guaranteeing the probabilities add to one.

items: A qubit state is a 2-entry complex vector [alpha, beta]
Add vectors entrywise; scale by a scalar
Norm must equal 1: |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1

content.text: A state vector is like a recipe: each entry is how much of each basis ingredient (|0> and |1>) to mix in.
The state 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> is the vector [0.6, 0.8]. Check the norm: 0.6^2 + 0.8^2 = 0.36 + 0.64 = 1, so it is a valid state. Measuring gives 0 with probability 0.36 and 1 with probability 0.64.

items: Using an un-normalised vector -- always check the entries squared add to 1.

modules.title: Unitary simulation

content.text: Every valid quantum gate is a unitary matrix. Unitarity is the single rule that keeps probabilities adding to one and makes all gates reversible.
A matrix U is unitary if U-dagger * U = I, where U-dagger is the conjugate transpose and I is the identity. Equivalently, the inverse of U equals its conjugate transpose.

Unitary operations preserve the length of vectors. Since a quantum state has length 1 and measurement probabilities come from squared lengths, unitarity is exactly what keeps the probabilities summing to 1 after any gate.

Because U-dagger undoes U, every gate is reversible: there is no information loss inside a quantum circuit until you measure. This is a deep difference from many classical logic gates like AND, which throw information away.

items: Unitary: U-dagger U = I
Inverse equals conjugate transpose
Preserves vector length (keeps probabilities = 1)
Every gate is reversible
Measurement is the only non-unitary step

content.text: A unitary is a rigid rotation of state space -- it can turn and reflect the arrow but never stretches or shrinks it.

U-dagger  U  =  I

(conjugate-transpose of U) times U = identity
Check H is unitary: H = (1/sqrt2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] is real and symmetric, so H-dagger = H. Then H*H = (1/2)[[2,0],[0,2]] = I. Unitary confirmed, and it shows H is its own inverse.

items: Assuming any matrix is a valid gate -- only unitary matrices are physically allowed.

modules.title: Building GHZ in code

content.text: The GHZ state is a three-or-more-qubit maximally entangled state. It generalises the Bell state and reveals even sharper non-classical behaviour.
The three-qubit GHZ state is (|000>+|111>)/sqrt2. All qubits are either all 0 or all 1, perfectly correlated. You build it with a Hadamard on the first qubit followed by a chain of CNOTs.

GHZ states show 'all-or-nothing' entanglement: measuring any one qubit instantly fixes all the others. They are used in multiparty protocols, quantum secret sharing and in dramatic tests of quantum mechanics that rule out local hidden-variable theories without needing statistics.
GHZ entanglement is also fragile: losing a single qubit destroys the entanglement of the whole state, which contrasts with more robust states like the W state.

items: GHZ: (|000>+|111>)/sqrt2 for 3 qubits
Built from H then a chain of CNOTs
All qubits perfectly correlated (all 0 or all 1)
Used in secret sharing and foundational tests
Fragile: losing one qubit breaks the entanglement

content.text: A GHZ state is like three dancers locked in step: they all step left together or all step right together, never out of sync.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(3, 3)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.cx(1, 2)                   # GHZ state
qc.measure(range(3), range(3))
Run the GHZ circuit for 1000 shots: you see about 500 '000' and 500 '111', and none of the other six outcomes -- confirming all-or-nothing correlation.

items: Expecting partial outcomes like '010' -- a perfect GHZ state only yields all-0 or all-1.

modules.title: Saving results and reproducibility

content.text: The four Bell states are the maximally entangled two-qubit states. They are the building blocks of entanglement-based protocols like teleportation and superdense coding.
There are four Bell states: (|00>+|11>)/sqrt2, (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, (|01>+|10>)/sqrt2 and (|01>-|10>)/sqrt2. Together they form an orthonormal basis for the two-qubit space, called the Bell basis.
You create the first Bell state with a Hadamard on the control followed by a CNOT. The other three come from first applying X or Z to one qubit, which flips the bit pattern or the sign.

A Bell measurement projects two qubits onto this basis and is the core operation in teleportation and entanglement swapping. Distinguishing the four Bell states is exactly how the receiver decodes information in superdense coding.

items: Four Bell states form the Bell basis
Built from H then CNOT (plus optional X/Z)
Maximally entangled two-qubit states
Bell measurement underlies teleportation
Superdense coding uses the four states to send 2 bits

content.text: The four Bell states are like four perfectly matched pairs of gloves -- knowing which pair you hold tells you everything about both gloves at once.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0)
qc.cx(0, 1)                # Phi+ Bell state
qc.measure([0,1], [0,1])
Starting from |10> (apply X to q0 first), H then CNOT produces (|00>-|11>)/sqrt2, the Phi-minus Bell state -- same correlations as Phi-plus but with a relative minus sign.

items: Mixing up which input basis state maps to which Bell state.

modules.title: Monaco-to-Qiskit workflow in QVANTA

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

items: Forgetting to add measurements, which leaves get_counts() with nothing to report.

modules.title: What is a quantum oracle

content.text: An oracle is a black-box subroutine that marks or evaluates inputs. Phase kickback is the mechanism that lets a quantum oracle write its answer into a phase rather than a bit.

An oracle Uf encodes a function f(x) reversibly. A common form is the phase oracle, which flips the sign of states where f(x) = 1, marking the target without changing measurement probabilities directly.

Phase kickback happens when the target qubit is prepared in the |-> state: applying a controlled operation then kicks a phase onto the control qubits instead of flipping the target. This is how Deutsch-Jozsa, Bernstein-Vazirani and Grover encode answers.

Oracles are an abstraction: in a real algorithm you must actually build the circuit that implements f, and its cost counts toward the total. The oracle model is useful for proving speed-ups independently of how f is built.

items: An oracle encodes a function reversibly
A phase oracle flips the sign of marked states
Phase kickback moves a phase onto the control qubits
Needs the target in |-> = (|0>-|1>)/sqrt2
Oracle cost counts in real algorithms

content.text: A phase oracle is like an invisible stamp that marks the right page with a hidden watermark you later reveal with interference.

target in |->:
control --*-- picks up phase (kickback)
          |
|->  ----[X]-- stays |->
Preparing the target in |-> and applying a CNOT controlled by |x> leaves the target unchanged but multiplies the control state by (-1)^x -- the phase has kicked back onto the control.

items: Forgetting to set the target to |-> first, which disables the kickback.

modules.title: The Deutsch problem

content.text: The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm was the first to show a clear, provable quantum advantage: it decides a global property of a function in a single query where classical methods may need exponentially many.

You are given a black-box function (oracle) that is promised to be either constant (same output for all inputs) or balanced (0 for half the inputs, 1 for the other half). Classically you may need to check just over half of all 2^n inputs to be sure. Deutsch-Jozsa answers with one quantum query.

The trick is to put all input qubits into superposition with Hadamards so the oracle acts on every input at once, encoding the answer as a phase (phase kickback). A second layer of Hadamards then makes the phases interfere.

After the final Hadamards, measuring all zeros means the function is constant, and any non-zero outcome means it is balanced. The exponential gap is dramatic, though the problem is somewhat artificial -- its real value is teaching phase kickback and interference.

items: Decides constant vs balanced in ONE query
Uses Hadamards to query all inputs at once
Relies on phase kickback and interference
All-zeros result = constant; anything else = balanced
First clear exponential quantum advantage

content.text: It is like weighing a bag of coins once to decide if they are all genuine or exactly half fake, instead of inspecting them one by one.

|0..0> -[H..H]- [ oracle Uf ] -[H..H]- measure
|1>    -[H]----             (phase kickback)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 1)
qc.x(1); qc.h([0,1])
# oracle for a balanced f: a CNOT
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.h(0); qc.measure(0, 0)   # result 1 => balanced
For the balanced oracle f(x) = x (a single CNOT), the algorithm measures 1 on the input qubit, correctly reporting 'balanced' after just one oracle call.

items: Forgetting to prepare the ancilla qubit in |1> via X before the Hadamards -- phase kickback needs it.

modules.title: The Deutsch algorithm circuit

content.text: The Deutsch-Jozsa algorithm was the first to show a clear, provable quantum advantage: it decides a global property of a function in a single query where classical methods may need exponentially many.

You are given a black-box function (oracle) that is promised to be either constant (same output for all inputs) or balanced (0 for half the inputs, 1 for the other half). Classically you may need to check just over half of all 2^n inputs to be sure. Deutsch-Jozsa answers with one quantum query.

The trick is to put all input qubits into superposition with Hadamards so the oracle acts on every input at once, encoding the answer as a phase (phase kickback). A second layer of Hadamards then makes the phases interfere.

After the final Hadamards, measuring all zeros means the function is constant, and any non-zero outcome means it is balanced. The exponential gap is dramatic, though the problem is somewhat artificial -- its real value is teaching phase kickback and interference.

items: Decides constant vs balanced in ONE query
Uses Hadamards to query all inputs at once
Relies on phase kickback and interference
All-zeros result = constant; anything else = balanced
First clear exponential quantum advantage

content.text: It is like weighing a bag of coins once to decide if they are all genuine or exactly half fake, instead of inspecting them one by one.

|0..0> -[H..H]- [ oracle Uf ] -[H..H]- measure
|1>    -[H]----             (phase kickback)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 1)
qc.x(1); qc.h([0,1])
# oracle for a balanced f: a CNOT
qc.cx(0, 1)
qc.h(0); qc.measure(0, 0)   # result 1 => balanced
For the balanced oracle f(x) = x (a single CNOT), the algorithm measures 1 on the input qubit, correctly reporting 'balanced' after just one oracle call.

items: Forgetting to prepare the ancilla qubit in |1> via X before the Hadamards -- phase kickback needs it.

modules.title: Bernstein-Vazirani problem

content.text: The Bernstein-Vazirani algorithm finds a hidden binary string inside an oracle with a single query, where a classical approach needs one query per bit.

The oracle computes f(x) = s . x (the bitwise dot product of a hidden string s with the input x, modulo 2). Classically you must query n times, once per bit, flipping a single input bit each time to read off each bit of s.

Quantumly you prepare all inputs in superposition, apply the oracle (which kicks the hidden bits into phases), apply Hadamards again, and measure. The measurement directly returns the entire hidden string s in one shot.
Like Deutsch-Jozsa, the engine is phase kickback plus Hadamard interference, but here the payoff is reading out a specific hidden value rather than a yes/no property.

items: Finds a hidden string s in ONE query (classically needs n)
Oracle computes s . x mod 2
Phase kickback encodes s into phases
Final Hadamards decode s directly on measurement

content.text: It is like discovering a secret combination lock's full code in a single pull, instead of testing each dial separately.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
s = '101'
qc = QuantumCircuit(len(s)+1, len(s))
qc.x(len(s)); qc.h(range(len(s)+1))
for i, bit in enumerate(reversed(s)):
    if bit == '1': qc.cx(i, len(s))
qc.h(range(len(s))); qc.measure(range(len(s)), range(len(s)))
For the hidden string s = 101, a single run measures '101' with certainty, recovering all three bits at once.

items: Reversing the bit order incorrectly when wiring the oracle CNOTs.

modules.title: Quantum vs classical query complexity

content.text: Quantum complexity theory classifies which problems quantum computers can solve efficiently and places them against classical classes like P and NP.

BQP (bounded-error quantum polynomial time) is the class of problems a quantum computer can solve efficiently with high probability. It contains P (efficient classical problems) and includes factoring, which is not known to be in P.

BQP is believed to be different from NP: quantum computers are not expected to solve NP-complete problems efficiently in general. Grover gives only a quadratic speed-up for search, far short of the exponential needed to crack NP-complete problems outright.
Complexity theory keeps quantum hype honest: it pinpoints where genuine speed-ups are proven or plausible (factoring, simulation) and where they are unlikely (general NP-complete problems).

items: BQP = efficiently quantum-solvable problems
P is inside BQP; factoring is in BQP
BQP is believed different from NP
No known efficient quantum solution to NP-complete problems
Grover gives only quadratic, not exponential, search speed-up

content.text: Complexity classes are like weight categories in sport: they tell you which problems a quantum computer is actually built to lift, and which stay out of reach.

P  subset  BQP
   NP (likely not inside BQP)
factoring in BQP, not known in P
Factoring sits in BQP thanks to Shor, yet is not known to be in P, which is precisely why a scalable quantum computer would be cryptographically disruptive.

items: Believing quantum computers solve all hard (NP-complete) problems quickly -- current theory says they most likely do not.

modules.title: Grover with unknown number of solutions

content.text: Grover's algorithm searches an unsorted database of N items in about sqrt(N) steps, a quadratic speed-up over the N/2 average of classical search.

Grover starts by putting all N = 2^n items into equal superposition with Hadamards. It then repeats a two-step Grover iteration: an oracle that flips the phase of the marked (correct) item, and a diffusion operator that reflects all amplitudes about their average.

Each iteration rotates the state a little closer to the marked item, increasing its measurement probability. After about (pi/4)*sqrt(N) iterations the marked item is very likely to be measured. Too many iterations overshoot and the probability drops again.

Grover is optimal for unstructured search: no quantum algorithm can do better than order sqrt(N). The quadratic speed-up is modest compared with exponential ones but applies to an enormous range of search and optimisation problems.

Grover iteration = oracle (phase flip) + diffusion (reflect about mean)
Optimal number of iterations is about (pi/4) sqrt(N)
Overshooting reduces success probability
Provably optimal for unstructured search

content.text: Amplitude amplification is like repeatedly nudging a spotlight so the marked item gets brighter and everything else dims, step by step.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h([0,1])
# oracle marks |11>:
qc.cz(0, 1)
# diffusion:
qc.h([0,1]); qc.x([0,1]); qc.cz(0,1); qc.x([0,1]); qc.h([0,1])
qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])   # measures 11 with high probability
For N = 4 (2 qubits) a single Grover iteration finds the marked item with 100 percent probability, because (pi/4)*sqrt(4) is about 1 iteration.

items: Running too many iterations -- the success probability oscillates, so more is not always better.

modules.title: Classical discrete Fourier transform

content.text: The Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) is the quantum version of the discrete Fourier transform. It is the engine inside phase estimation and Shor's algorithm.

The QFT maps a basis state |x> to a superposition whose amplitudes have phases proportional to x, effectively converting information encoded in computational-basis values into information encoded in phases (the frequency domain).

On n qubits the QFT uses n Hadamards and a pattern of controlled-phase rotations, followed by qubit reversals (swaps). It needs only about n^2 gates, compared with the N*log N operations of the classical fast Fourier transform on N = 2^n amplitudes -- an exponential improvement in gate count.

The catch is that you cannot read all the transformed amplitudes directly; measurement gives only one outcome. The QFT is powerful only as a subroutine where later interference extracts a single useful number, such as a period or a phase.

items: Quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform
Moves information between value and phase (frequency) domains
Needs about n^2 gates on n qubits
Uses Hadamards plus controlled-phase rotations
Key subroutine of phase estimation and Shor

content.text: The QFT is like a prism that splits a signal into its frequencies -- but you only get to sample one frequency when you measure.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.circuit.library import QFT
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.append(QFT(3), range(3))
print(qc.decompose())
The QFT of the uniform state is a single computational basis state, and the QFT of a periodic state concentrates amplitude on frequencies matching the period -- exactly what Shor exploits.

items: Expecting to read the whole spectrum -- measurement collapses to one frequency per run.

modules.title: QFT on one qubit

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

modules.title: The swap step

content.text: This module explains the SWAP gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.
The SWAP gate exchanges the full quantum states of two qubits, so |01> becomes |10> and vice versa. The |00> and |11> states are unchanged.
SWAP can be built from three CNOTs: CX(a,b) then CX(b,a) then CX(a,b). This matters because real hardware rarely has a native SWAP, and swapping costs three two-qubit gates.
SWAPs are inserted automatically by the transpiler to move logical qubits next to each other when the hardware has limited connectivity, so understanding SWAP helps you reason about circuit overhead.
Action: Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
On the Bloch sphere: Two-qubit gate.

items: Symbol: SWAP
Exchanges the states of the two qubits: |01> <-> |10>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
Two-qubit gate.

modules.title: Inverse QFT

content.text: The Quantum Fourier Transform (QFT) is the quantum version of the discrete Fourier transform. It is the engine inside phase estimation and Shor's algorithm.

The QFT maps a basis state |x> to a superposition whose amplitudes have phases proportional to x, effectively converting information encoded in computational-basis values into information encoded in phases (the frequency domain).

On n qubits the QFT uses n Hadamards and a pattern of controlled-phase rotations, followed by qubit reversals (swaps). It needs only about n^2 gates, compared with the N*log N operations of the classical fast Fourier transform on N = 2^n amplitudes -- an exponential improvement in gate count.

The catch is that you cannot read all the transformed amplitudes directly; measurement gives only one outcome. The QFT is powerful only as a subroutine where later interference extracts a single useful number, such as a period or a phase.

items: Quantum analogue of the discrete Fourier transform
Moves information between value and phase (frequency) domains
Needs about n^2 gates on n qubits
Uses Hadamards plus controlled-phase rotations
Key subroutine of phase estimation and Shor

content.text: The QFT is like a prism that splits a signal into its frequencies -- but you only get to sample one frequency when you measure.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit.circuit.library import QFT
qc = QuantumCircuit(3)
qc.append(QFT(3), range(3))
print(qc.decompose())
The QFT of the uniform state is a single computational basis state, and the QFT of a periodic state concentrates amplitude on frequencies matching the period -- exactly what Shor exploits.

modules.title: Eigenvalues and phases

content.text: Eigenvectors are the special states a gate leaves pointing in the same direction, and eigenvalues say by how much they are scaled. They explain gate behaviour and are central to phase estimation.
For a matrix A, an eigenvector v satisfies A*v = lambda*v, where the number lambda is the eigenvalue. The gate does not rotate v into a new direction, it only scales it by lambda.
For a unitary gate every eigenvalue has magnitude 1, so it can be written as e^(i*theta). The phase theta is exactly what the phase-estimation algorithm is designed to read out.

Eigen-decomposition lets you understand a gate by its action on its eigenvectors. For example, Z has eigenvector |0> with eigenvalue +1 and eigenvector |1> with eigenvalue -1, which is just a restatement of Z|0>=|0> and Z|1>=-|1>.

items: A*v = lambda*v: v is the eigenvector, lambda the eigenvalue
Unitary eigenvalues have magnitude 1 (e^(i*theta))
Eigenvectors are directions the gate only scales
Phase estimation reads the eigenvalue phase

content.text: Eigenvectors are the axes a spinning object can rotate around without wobbling -- the object just turns along them cleanly.
For Z, |1> is an eigenvector: Z|1> = -|1>, so the eigenvalue is -1 = e^(i*pi). Its phase pi is what phase estimation would return.

items: Expecting a gate to rotate its own eigenvectors -- it only scales them.

modules.title: The phase estimation problem

content.text: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) reads out the phase of an eigenvalue of a unitary. It is a central subroutine of Shor's algorithm and quantum chemistry.

Given a unitary U and one of its eigenstates |u> with eigenvalue e^(2*pi*i*phase), QPE estimates the unknown phase. It uses a register of counting qubits in superposition and applies controlled powers of U so the phase is written into their relative phases.
An inverse QFT on the counting register then converts those relative phases into a binary number you can measure. More counting qubits give more bits of precision in the phase estimate.
QPE is the workhorse behind Shor's period finding and behind estimating molecular energies, because many problems reduce to 'find the eigenvalue phase of this operator'.

items: Estimates the phase of a unitary's eigenvalue
Uses counting qubits plus controlled powers of U
An inverse QFT converts phases into a readable number
More counting qubits = more precision
Core of Shor and of energy estimation

content.text: QPE is like timing how fast a spinning wheel turns by taking several snapshots at doubling intervals, then reading the rotation rate from the pattern.

counting |0..0> -[H..H]-[ c-U^(2^k) ]-[ inverse QFT ]- measure
eigenstate |u> ----------[   U powers  ]----------- |u>

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
# sketch: controlled-U powers on counting register, then inverse QFT
qc = QuantumCircuit(4, 3)
qc.h([0,1,2]); qc.x(3)
# (apply controlled-U^(2^k) here), then inverse QFT on [0,1,2]
qc.measure([0,1,2],[0,1,2])
If U is the Z-like phase gate with eigenvalue e^(2*pi*i*0.25) on |1>, a 2-qubit QPE measures the binary fraction 0.01 = 0.25, correctly recovering the phase.

items: Using too few counting qubits to resolve the phase, giving a coarse or wrong estimate.

modules.title: Precision and number of ancilla qubits

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: Every valid quantum gate is a unitary matrix. Unitarity is the single rule that keeps probabilities adding to one and makes all gates reversible.
A matrix U is unitary if U-dagger * U = I, where U-dagger is the conjugate transpose and I is the identity. Equivalently, the inverse of U equals its conjugate transpose.

Unitary operations preserve the length of vectors. Since a quantum state has length 1 and measurement probabilities come from squared lengths, unitarity is exactly what keeps the probabilities summing to 1 after any gate.

Because U-dagger undoes U, every gate is reversible: there is no information loss inside a quantum circuit until you measure. This is a deep difference from many classical logic gates like AND, which throw information away.

items: Unitary: U-dagger U = I
Inverse equals conjugate transpose
Preserves vector length (keeps probabilities = 1)
Every gate is reversible
Measurement is the only non-unitary step

content.text: A unitary is a rigid rotation of state space -- it can turn and reflect the arrow but never stretches or shrinks it.

U-dagger  U  =  I

(conjugate-transpose of U) times U = identity
Check H is unitary: H = (1/sqrt2)[[1,1],[1,-1]] is real and symmetric, so H-dagger = H. Then H*H = (1/2)[[2,0],[0,2]] = I. Unitary confirmed, and it shows H is its own inverse.

items: Assuming any matrix is a valid gate -- only unitary matrices are physically allowed.

modules.title: Phase estimation error analysis

content.text: Quantum Phase Estimation (QPE) reads out the phase of an eigenvalue of a unitary. It is a central subroutine of Shor's algorithm and quantum chemistry.

Given a unitary U and one of its eigenstates |u> with eigenvalue e^(2*pi*i*phase), QPE estimates the unknown phase. It uses a register of counting qubits in superposition and applies controlled powers of U so the phase is written into their relative phases.
An inverse QFT on the counting register then converts those relative phases into a binary number you can measure. More counting qubits give more bits of precision in the phase estimate.
QPE is the workhorse behind Shor's period finding and behind estimating molecular energies, because many problems reduce to 'find the eigenvalue phase of this operator'.

items: Estimates the phase of a unitary's eigenvalue
Uses counting qubits plus controlled powers of U
An inverse QFT converts phases into a readable number
More counting qubits = more precision
Core of Shor and of energy estimation

content.text: QPE is like timing how fast a spinning wheel turns by taking several snapshots at doubling intervals, then reading the rotation rate from the pattern.

counting |0..0> -[H..H]-[ c-U^(2^k) ]-[ inverse QFT ]- measure
eigenstate |u> ----------[   U powers  ]----------- |u>

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
# sketch: controlled-U powers on counting register, then inverse QFT
qc = QuantumCircuit(4, 3)
qc.h([0,1,2]); qc.x(3)
# (apply controlled-U^(2^k) here), then inverse QFT on [0,1,2]
qc.measure([0,1,2],[0,1,2])
If U is the Z-like phase gate with eigenvalue e^(2*pi*i*0.25) on |1>, a 2-qubit QPE measures the binary fraction 0.01 = 0.25, correctly recovering the phase.

items: Using too few counting qubits to resolve the phase, giving a coarse or wrong estimate.

modules.title: RSA and why factoring matters

content.text: Shor's algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA encryption. It reduces factoring to period-finding, which a quantum computer solves efficiently with the QFT.

To factor N, Shor picks a random a coprime to N and looks for the period r of the function f(x) = a^x mod N, meaning the smallest r with a^r = 1 mod N. Finding r is the hard part classically, but easy quantumly.

The quantum core prepares a superposition over x, computes a^x mod N into a second register, and applies the QFT to extract the period r via phase estimation. Once r is known (and is even, with a^(r/2) not equal to -1 mod N), the factors come from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N).

Because the best known classical factoring algorithms are sub-exponential while Shor is polynomial, a large fault-tolerant quantum computer could break RSA and related public-key cryptography. This is the main driver of post-quantum cryptography.

items: Factors integers in polynomial time
Reduces factoring to finding the period of a^x mod N
Quantum period-finding uses the QFT
Factors from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N)
Breaks RSA, driving post-quantum cryptography

content.text: Shor is like finding the exact repeat length of a wallpaper pattern by looking at it through a frequency prism, then using that repeat to unlock the secret.

classical: pick a, compute gcd
   |
quantum: period r of a^x mod N  (QFT + phase estimation)
   |
classical: factors = gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N)

# Shor is heavy; Qiskit historically provided Shor in qiskit.algorithms.
# Conceptually:
# 1) pick random a coprime to N
# 2) quantum order-finding of a^x mod N via QFT
# 3) classical gcd to extract factors
N = 15   # example: factors into 3 and 5
For N = 15 with a = 7, the period of 7^x mod 15 is r = 4. Then gcd(7^2 - 1, 15) = gcd(48,15) = 3 and gcd(7^2 + 1, 15) = gcd(50,15) = 5, giving the factors 3 and 5.

items: Forgetting the classical pre- and post-processing -- Shor is a hybrid algorithm, not purely quantum.

modules.title: Full Shor pipeline

content.text: Shor's algorithm factors large integers in polynomial time, threatening RSA encryption. It reduces factoring to period-finding, which a quantum computer solves efficiently with the QFT.

To factor N, Shor picks a random a coprime to N and looks for the period r of the function f(x) = a^x mod N, meaning the smallest r with a^r = 1 mod N. Finding r is the hard part classically, but easy quantumly.

The quantum core prepares a superposition over x, computes a^x mod N into a second register, and applies the QFT to extract the period r via phase estimation. Once r is known (and is even, with a^(r/2) not equal to -1 mod N), the factors come from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N).

Because the best known classical factoring algorithms are sub-exponential while Shor is polynomial, a large fault-tolerant quantum computer could break RSA and related public-key cryptography. This is the main driver of post-quantum cryptography.

items: Factors integers in polynomial time
Reduces factoring to finding the period of a^x mod N
Quantum period-finding uses the QFT
Factors from gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N)
Breaks RSA, driving post-quantum cryptography

content.text: Shor is like finding the exact repeat length of a wallpaper pattern by looking at it through a frequency prism, then using that repeat to unlock the secret.

classical: pick a, compute gcd
   |
quantum: period r of a^x mod N  (QFT + phase estimation)
   |
classical: factors = gcd(a^(r/2) +/- 1, N)

# Shor is heavy; Qiskit historically provided Shor in qiskit.algorithms.
# Conceptually:
# 1) pick random a coprime to N
# 2) quantum order-finding of a^x mod N via QFT
# 3) classical gcd to extract factors
N = 15   # example: factors into 3 and 5
For N = 15 with a = 7, the period of 7^x mod 15 is r = 4. Then gcd(7^2 - 1, 15) = gcd(48,15) = 3 and gcd(7^2 + 1, 15) = gcd(50,15) = 5, giving the factors 3 and 5.

modules.title: Impact on cryptography

content.text: Rotation gates turn a qubit by an arbitrary angle about an axis of the Bloch sphere. They generalise the fixed Pauli gates and build any single-qubit operation.

RX(theta), RY(theta) and RZ(theta) rotate the Bloch-sphere state by angle theta about the X, Y and Z axes respectively. The fixed gates are special cases: X = RX(pi) up to a phase, and Z relates to RZ(pi).

RY(theta) is especially handy because it keeps amplitudes real: RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>, letting you dial any desired split between 0 and 1. RZ changes only the relative phase.

Any single-qubit gate can be written as a product of rotations, for example using the U(theta, phi, lambda) gate with three angles. This is the basis of how compilers express arbitrary operations with hardware-native rotations.

items: RX, RY, RZ rotate by any angle about X, Y, Z
Angles are in radians
RY(theta)|0> = cos(theta/2)|0> + sin(theta/2)|1>
RZ changes relative phase only
Any 1-qubit gate = product of rotations

content.text: Rotation gates are like steering a ball on a globe by a precise number of degrees, rather than only flipping it to the opposite pole.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
import numpy as np
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.ry(np.pi/3, 0)   # 60-degree rotation about Y
qc.measure(0, 0)    # P(1) = sin^2(30deg) = 0.25
RY(pi/2) on |0> gives cos(45deg)|0> + sin(45deg)|1> = (|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 = |+>, so a 90-degree Y-rotation reproduces the Hadamard's superposition (up to phase).

items: Supplying the angle in degrees instead of radians.
Forgetting the half-angle in the cos/sin amplitudes.

modules.title: Post-quantum cryptography overview

content.text: Quantum key distribution lets two parties share a secret key whose security rests on the laws of physics: any eavesdropper necessarily disturbs the quantum states and is detected.

In BB84, Alice sends qubits each prepared in a randomly chosen basis (Z or X) encoding a random bit. Bob measures each in a randomly chosen basis. Afterwards they publicly compare which bases they used and keep only the bits where the bases matched.

Security comes from measurement disturbance and no-cloning: an eavesdropper who measures the qubits must guess the basis, and wrong guesses introduce detectable errors. By sampling some of their shared bits, Alice and Bob can estimate the error rate and detect eavesdropping.

E91 is a variant using entangled pairs and Bell-inequality violations to certify security. Both contrast with Shor's threat to classical cryptography, which is why quantum-safe key exchange is of strong practical interest.

items: Shares a secret key with physics-based security
Alice/Bob each pick random bases (Z or X)
Keep bits only where bases matched (sifting)
Eavesdropping disturbs states and is detectable
E91 uses entanglement and Bell tests

content.text: BB84 is like sending messages written in disappearing ink that smudges if anyone peeks, so the recipients can tell whether it was intercepted.

Alice: random bit + random basis -> qubit --> Bob: random basis measure
keep bits where bases agree; check a sample for eavesdropping
If Alice sends 1 in the X basis (state |->), and Bob measures in the Z basis, his result is random -- so mismatched-basis bits are discarded, and only matching-basis bits form the key.

items: Forgetting the sifting step -- bits from mismatched bases are useless and must be dropped.

modules.title: Parameterized quantum circuits (ansatz)

content.text: Qiskit is IBM's open-source Python SDK for building, simulating and running quantum circuits. This module shows the standard build-run-read workflow.

You build a circuit with QuantumCircuit(n_qubits, n_classical_bits), add gates with methods like qc.h(0) and qc.cx(0,1), and add measurements with qc.measure. The circuit is just a Python object describing the operations.

To run it you choose a backend. The Aer simulator runs the circuit on your own machine; real IBM hardware runs it on physical qubits. Before hardware, the transpiler rewrites your circuit into the device's native gates and connectivity.
You run with a number of shots (repetitions) and read the results with get_counts(), which returns a dictionary of outcome strings to how often they occurred -- exactly the histogram QVANTA displays.

items: QuantumCircuit(n, m): n qubits, m classical bits
Add gates: qc.h, qc.x, qc.cx, qc.measure
Simulate with Aer; transpile for real hardware
Run with 'shots' repetitions
get_counts() returns the outcome histogram

content.text: Qiskit is like a music score editor: you place the notes (gates), then press play on an instrument (simulator or hardware) to hear the result (counts).

build -> transpile -> run(shots) -> get_counts()
  qc        native       backend      histogram

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit, transpile
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(2, 2)
qc.h(0); qc.cx(0, 1); qc.measure([0,1],[0,1])
sim = AerSimulator()
job = sim.run(transpile(qc, sim), shots=1024)
print(job.result().get_counts())
Running the Bell circuit above for 1024 shots prints something like {'00': 512, '11': 512}, confirming the entangled correlation.

modules.title: Cost functions and expectation values

content.text: Measurement outcomes are random, and the Born rule tells you their probabilities. This is the bridge from a quantum state to the histogram the simulator shows you.

The Born rule states that the probability of measuring a particular basis outcome equals the squared magnitude of that outcome's amplitude. For alpha|0> + beta|1>, you get 0 with probability |alpha|^2 and 1 with probability |beta|^2.

Because the state is normalised, these probabilities add to 1. A single measurement gives one random outcome and collapses the state; to see the full distribution you run many shots and build a histogram.
The expectation value is the average outcome weighted by probability. For an observable it is computed as <psi|A|psi> and is what many algorithms, such as VQE, actually try to minimise.

items: Probability = |amplitude|^2 (Born rule)
Probabilities add to 1
One shot gives one random outcome and collapses the state
Many shots build a histogram
Expectation value = <psi|A|psi>

content.text: A quantum state is like a weighted dice: the amplitudes squared are the chances of each face, and each roll (shot) gives just one face.

state: alpha|0> + beta|1>

P(0) = |alpha|^2
P(1) = |beta|^2
P(0) + P(1) = 1
For (|0> + i|1>)/sqrt2, alpha = 1/sqrt2 and beta = i/sqrt2. P(0) = |1/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5 and P(1) = |i/sqrt2|^2 = 0.5, so the histogram over many shots is about half 0 and half 1.

items: Using the amplitude itself instead of its squared magnitude for the probability.
Forgetting that a phase like i does not change a single-measurement probability.

modules.title: The variational loop

content.text: VQE is a hybrid quantum-classical algorithm that estimates the lowest energy (ground state) of a system. It is one of the most practical algorithms for today's noisy hardware.

VQE uses a parameterised circuit called an ansatz that prepares a trial state depending on tunable angles. The quantum computer measures the energy (expectation value of the Hamiltonian) of that trial state.

A classical optimiser then adjusts the angles to lower the measured energy, looping until it converges on the minimum. The variational principle guarantees the true ground-state energy is a lower bound, so the best you find is an estimate from above.

Because the circuits are shallow and errors partly average out, VQE suits near-term devices. It is the leading approach for quantum chemistry and materials, estimating molecular ground-state energies.

items: Hybrid: quantum circuit plus classical optimiser
Ansatz prepares a tunable trial state
Measures energy = expectation of the Hamiltonian
Optimiser minimises the energy
Variational principle: result is an upper bound on the true ground energy

content.text: VQE is like tuning a guitar string by ear: you pluck (measure energy), adjust the peg (parameters), and repeat until it is as low as it goes.

+--> ansatz(theta) --> measure energy --+
  |                                       |
  +---- classical optimiser updates theta +

# sketch with Qiskit primitives
# 1) define Hamiltonian H
# 2) define ansatz circuit with parameters theta
# 3) estimator.run(ansatz, H, theta) -> energy
# 4) classical optimiser minimises energy over theta
For the hydrogen molecule H2 at its bond length, VQE with a small ansatz converges to a ground-state energy near -1.137 Hartree, matching the known value.

modules.title: Hamiltonians and Pauli decomposition

content.text: Simulating molecules and materials is one of the most promising applications of quantum computers, because quantum systems are naturally hard for classical machines but natural for quantum ones.

The behaviour of a molecule is governed by its Hamiltonian, an operator whose lowest eigenvalue is the ground-state energy that determines chemistry such as reaction rates and bond strengths. Classically, the cost of solving this grows exponentially with the number of electrons.

To put a molecule on a quantum computer you map its fermionic Hamiltonian onto qubits using transformations like Jordan-Wigner or Bravyi-Kitaev. Then VQE or phase estimation finds the ground-state energy.

Even modest quantum computers may eventually simulate molecules beyond classical reach, helping design catalysts, batteries and drugs. This is widely seen as the application most likely to deliver real quantum advantage.

items: A molecule's Hamiltonian encodes its energy
Ground-state energy drives chemistry
Classical cost grows exponentially with electrons
Map fermions to qubits (Jordan-Wigner, Bravyi-Kitaev)
Solve with VQE or phase estimation

content.text: Simulating a molecule classically is like predicting a crowd's every move by tracking each person; a quantum computer lets the crowd simulate itself.
molecule -> Hamiltonian H -> map to qubits -> VQE/QPE -> ground energy

# sketch: build molecular Hamiltonian (e.g. via a chemistry package),
# map to qubit operators, then run VQE to estimate ground-state energy
The hydrogen molecule H2 in a minimal basis maps to a few-qubit Hamiltonian; VQE recovers its ground-state energy curve as a function of bond length, reproducing the known dissociation curve.

modules.title: QAOA overview

content.text: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a hybrid algorithm for combinatorial optimisation problems like MaxCut, designed for near-term hardware.

QAOA encodes an optimisation problem as a cost Hamiltonian whose lowest-energy state is the best solution. It alternates applying a cost layer (which imprints the problem) and a mixer layer (which explores alternatives), each controlled by an angle.

A classical optimiser tunes those angles to maximise the probability of measuring a good solution. Increasing the number of layers p improves quality but also deepens the circuit and its sensitivity to noise.
QAOA is a leading candidate for showing near-term quantum usefulness in optimisation, though whether it beats the best classical heuristics remains an active research question.

items: Hybrid algorithm for combinatorial optimisation
Encodes the problem as a cost Hamiltonian
Alternates cost and mixer layers (p layers)
Classical optimiser tunes the layer angles
More layers = better quality but deeper, noisier circuit

content.text: QAOA is like alternately pushing a ball toward a goal (cost layer) and jiggling the table (mixer) so it does not get stuck in a dip before reaching the lowest point.

|+...+> -[cost(gamma1)]-[mixer(beta1)]-...-[measure]
          repeated for p layers, angles optimised classically

# sketch: build cost + mixer layers for MaxCut
# vary (gamma, beta) angles with a classical optimiser
# measure bitstrings; the most frequent good cut is the answer
For MaxCut on a triangle graph, QAOA with p = 1 already concentrates measurement outcomes on the cuts that separate the graph into the two best partitions.

modules.title: Why qubits need protection

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

modules.title: Decoherence and noise sources

content.text: Decoherence is the process by which a qubit loses its quantum behaviour to its environment. T1 and T2 are the timescales that quantify it on real hardware.

T1 is the energy-relaxation time: how long a qubit stays in |1> before decaying toward |0>, losing energy to its surroundings. T2 is the dephasing time: how long the delicate relative phase of a superposition survives. Always T2 is at most 2*T1.
Because gates take time, every operation spends some of the T1/T2 budget, and longer circuits accumulate more decoherence. This is why near-term (NISQ) algorithms are kept shallow.

Noise is modelled with channels such as depolarising, amplitude damping (T1) and phase damping (T2). Qiskit Aer can simulate with a noise model so you can predict how a real device will degrade your results before running on hardware.

items: T1 = energy relaxation (|1> decays to |0>)
T2 = dephasing (loss of phase coherence)
Always T2 <= 2*T1
Longer circuits accumulate more decoherence
Model with depolarising, amplitude-damping, phase-damping channels

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning top: T1 is how long before it falls over (loses energy), T2 is how long before its wobble (phase) becomes unpredictable.

|1> --T1--> |0>        (energy relaxation)
phase coherence --T2--> lost  (dephasing)

from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error
nm = NoiseModel()
nm.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.02, 1), ['h','x'])
sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=nm)   # simulate with noise
If a device has T1 = 100 microseconds and your circuit takes 10 microseconds, roughly 10 percent of the |1> population may have decayed, visibly shifting your histogram toward 0.

modules.title: Bit-flip errors

content.text: This module explains the Pauli-X (NOT / bit-flip) gate in full: what it does to a qubit, its matrix form, how it looks on the Bloch sphere, runnable Qiskit code, and a worked numerical example.

The Pauli-X gate is the quantum version of the classical NOT gate. It flips the computational basis states: it turns |0> into |1> and |1> into |0>. For a general qubit alpha|0> + beta|1>, it swaps the two amplitudes, giving beta|0> + alpha|1>.
Geometrically, X is a 180-degree rotation of the Bloch sphere about the X-axis. The north pole (|0>) and south pole (|1>) swap places, which is exactly why it behaves like a bit-flip.

X is both Hermitian (equal to its own conjugate transpose) and unitary, and it is its own inverse: applying X twice returns the original state because X*X = I. This makes it a very safe gate to experiment with.
Action: X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
On the Bloch sphere: 180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

items: Symbol: X
X|0> = |1>, X|1> = |0>; on alpha|0>+beta|1> it gives beta|0>+alpha|1>.
Unitary (U-dagger U = I), so it is reversible.
180-degree rotation about the Bloch X-axis.

content.text: Picture this idea as one clear step that builds directly on the previous module.

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.x(0)            # bit-flip: |0> -> |1>
qc.measure(0, 0)   # you will measure 1 with certainty
Now take 0.6|0> + 0.8|1> = [0.6, 0.8]. After X we get [0.8, 0.6] = 0.8|0> + 0.6|1>: the measurement probabilities 0 and 1 have swapped from 0.36/0.64 to 0.64/0.36.

items: Thinking X changes phase -- it does not, it only swaps the |0> and |1> amplitudes.
Confusing X (bit-flip) with Z (phase-flip).

modules.title: Syndrome measurement

content.text: Measurement is how a quantum state becomes a classical result. It is probabilistic, irreversible, and the only non-unitary step in a quantum circuit.

When you measure a qubit in the computational basis, you get 0 or 1 with probabilities given by the Born rule (|amplitude|^2). The act of measuring collapses the state onto the outcome you saw: after measuring 1, the qubit is now exactly |1>.

Collapse is irreversible and destroys the superposition, so you cannot read the amplitudes directly. To learn the distribution you prepare and measure the same circuit many times (shots) and build a histogram of outcomes.
You can measure in other bases too. Measuring in the X basis is done by applying a Hadamard first and then measuring in the Z basis, which is how you probe phase information that the Z basis hides.

items: Outcome probability = |amplitude|^2
Measurement collapses the state onto the result
It is irreversible and destroys superposition
Repeat many shots to see the distribution
Change basis by rotating before measuring

content.text: Measurement is like opening a wrapped gift: before opening, several possibilities exist; opening fixes one and you cannot un-open it.

(|0>+|1>)/sqrt2 --[measure]--> 0  (state now |0>)
                           or  1  (state now |1>)

from qiskit import QuantumCircuit
from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
qc = QuantumCircuit(1, 1)
qc.h(0)
qc.measure(0, 0)
result = AerSimulator().run(qc, shots=1000).result()
print(result.get_counts())   # about {'0': 500, '1': 500}
Measuring |+> once might give 0; the qubit then collapses to |0>, and measuring again immediately gives 0 with certainty. The randomness was in the first measurement only.

items: Expecting a single measurement to reveal the amplitudes -- it only gives one random outcome.

modules.title: Stabilizer formalism intuition

content.text: Quantum error correction protects fragile quantum information by spreading one logical qubit across many physical qubits, so errors can be detected and fixed without measuring the data directly.

Qubits decohere and gates are imperfect, so raw quantum states degrade quickly. Error correction encodes a single logical qubit into an entangled block of physical qubits. The no-cloning theorem forbids simply copying the state, so codes use redundancy in a cleverer, entangled way.

Errors are detected using stabiliser measurements, which reveal a syndrome (which error occurred) without collapsing the encoded information. The simplest example, the three-qubit repetition code, protects against a single bit-flip by majority vote. The nine-qubit Shor code handles both bit and phase flips.

The surface code is today's leading practical scheme because it tolerates relatively high error rates and needs only nearest-neighbour connectivity. Below a threshold error rate, adding more physical qubits exponentially suppresses the logical error -- the foundation of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

modules.title: The 5-qubit code

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

modules.title: Coherence times T1 and T2

content.text: Decoherence is the process by which a qubit loses its quantum behaviour to its environment. T1 and T2 are the timescales that quantify it on real hardware.

T1 is the energy-relaxation time: how long a qubit stays in |1> before decaying toward |0>, losing energy to its surroundings. T2 is the dephasing time: how long the delicate relative phase of a superposition survives. Always T2 is at most 2*T1.
Because gates take time, every operation spends some of the T1/T2 budget, and longer circuits accumulate more decoherence. This is why near-term (NISQ) algorithms are kept shallow.

Noise is modelled with channels such as depolarising, amplitude damping (T1) and phase damping (T2). Qiskit Aer can simulate with a noise model so you can predict how a real device will degrade your results before running on hardware.

items: T1 = energy relaxation (|1> decays to |0>)
T2 = dephasing (loss of phase coherence)
Always T2 <= 2*T1
Longer circuits accumulate more decoherence
Model with depolarising, amplitude-damping, phase-damping channels

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning top: T1 is how long before it falls over (loses energy), T2 is how long before its wobble (phase) becomes unpredictable.

|1> --T1--> |0>        (energy relaxation)
phase coherence --T2--> lost  (dephasing)

from qiskit_aer import AerSimulator
from qiskit_aer.noise import NoiseModel, depolarizing_error
nm = NoiseModel()
nm.add_all_qubit_quantum_error(depolarizing_error(0.02, 1), ['h','x'])
sim = AerSimulator(noise_model=nm)   # simulate with noise
If a device has T1 = 100 microseconds and your circuit takes 10 microseconds, roughly 10 percent of the |1> population may have decayed, visibly shifting your histogram toward 0.

items: Assuming simulator results match hardware -- without a noise model the simulator is perfect and too optimistic.

modules.title: Gate errors and fidelity

content.text: Benchmarking and verification measure how good a quantum device really is and whether you can trust its results, which is essential before believing any quantum computation.

Randomised benchmarking applies random sequences of Clifford gates that should return the qubits to the start, then measures how quickly fidelity decays with sequence length. This gives an average gate error robust to measurement errors.

Quantum volume is a single number summarising a device's usable size, combining qubit count, connectivity, gate fidelity and more by testing the largest square random circuit the device can run reliably.

Tomography fully reconstructs a state (state tomography) or an operation (process tomography) from many measurements, giving a complete but expensive picture. Together these tools verify hardware claims and track improvement over time.

items: Randomised benchmarking gives average gate error
Robust to state-prep and measurement errors
Quantum volume summarises usable device size
Tomography reconstructs full states or processes (expensive)
Used to verify and trust quantum results

content.text: Benchmarking is like a car's standardised test track: it tells you real performance in comparable numbers, not just the brochure's claims.

random Clifford sequence -> inverse -> measure
fidelity decays with length -> average gate error
If randomised benchmarking shows fidelity dropping by 0.1 percent per gate, the average gate error is about 0.001, letting you estimate how deep a circuit can run before results become noise.

items: Reading a single high two-qubit fidelity as proof the whole device is good -- quantum volume and full benchmarking give the real picture.

modules.title: Qubit connectivity constraints

content.text: The qubit is the fundamental unit of quantum information. Unlike a bit it can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1, and this module explains exactly what that means.

A qubit's state is written alpha|0> + beta|1>, where |0> and |1> are the two basis states and alpha, beta are complex amplitudes. The amplitudes must satisfy |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1 so the probabilities add to one.

When alpha and beta are both non-zero the qubit is in superposition: it has a well-defined quantum state that is genuinely a blend of 0 and 1, not a hidden secret value. Only measurement forces it to a single outcome.

Physically a qubit can be built from many systems -- a superconducting circuit, a trapped ion, a photon's polarisation -- but mathematically they are all the same two-level quantum system described by the same vector.

items: State: alpha|0> + beta|1> with |alpha|^2 + |beta|^2 = 1
Superposition is a real blend of 0 and 1
Measurement collapses it to a single outcome
Many physical realisations, one mathematical model

content.text: A qubit is like a spinning coin in the air: while spinning it is neither heads nor tails but a blend, and only when it lands (measurement) does it become one.

|0>
        |
        |   * qubit state
        |  /
        | /
        |/
 -------+------- |1> direction (south pole)
The state (sqrt(3)/2)|0> + (1/2)|1> is valid because (3/4) + (1/4) = 1. Measuring gives 0 with probability 3/4 and 1 with probability 1/4.

items: Thinking the qubit secretly already is 0 or 1 before measurement -- superposition is physically real.
